title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 Overview
This section covers Part 1 - Introduction: what a time series is, components, stationarity, white noise, benchmark forecasts and forecast accuracy. The main ideas here are,

title: 1  Introduction
text:
A time series is one realisation of a stochastic process. The observations are dependent, so the usual iid methods don’t work.
Components: trend (long term change), seasonality (fixed known period, e.g. 12 months), cycle (rises and falls with no fixed period), irregular (noise).
Weak stationarity: constant mean, constant variance, and the autocovariance only depends on the lag, not on time.

Trend → difference: \(\nabla y_t = y_t - y_{t-1}\)
Seasonality → seasonal difference: \(\nabla_m y_t = y_t - y_{t-m}\)
Variance grows with the level → take logs (or a Box-Cox transform)

Lag operator: \(B y_t = y_{t-1}\), so \(\nabla = 1 - B\) and \(\nabla_m = 1 - B^m\).
White noise: mean 0, constant variance, no autocorrelation. The residuals of a good model should look like white noise. Test with Ljung-Box (H0: no autocorrelation up to lag h).
Benchmarks: mean, naive (\(\hat y_{T+h} = y_T\)), seasonal naive (same value as last season), drift (naive plus the average change). A model is only useful if it beats these.
Accuracy: always measure on data the model has not seen (a test set at the end of the series, never a random split). RMSE, MAE, MAPE and MASE (MASE below 1 means better than naive). Time series cross validation uses a rolling forecast origin.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 Worked Example

1.2.1 Look at the data


Code
library(forecast)
library(tseries)

y <- AirPassengers   # monthly airline passengers 1949-1960
plot(y, main = "Air passengers")









The trend goes up, there is a yearly pattern, and the seasonal swings get bigger as the level goes up. So take logs first.


Code
plot(log(y), main = "log(Air passengers)")









Code
# STL decomposition into trend, season and remainder
plot(stl(log(y), s.window = "periodic"))











1.2.2 Stationarity


Code
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
acf(log(y), lag.max = 48, main = "log(y)")
acf(diff(log(y)), lag.max = 48, main = "first difference")
acf(diff(diff(log(y)), lag = 12), lag.max = 48, main = "first + seasonal diff")









Code
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))


The ACF of log(y) decays very slowly, which is the sign of a trend (non-stationary). After the first difference, there are still big spikes at lags 12, 24, 36 (seasonality). After both differences, it looks close to stationary.
Two tests that work in opposite directions:

ADF: H0 = unit root (non-stationary). Small p-value means stationary.
KPSS: H0 = stationary. Small p-value means non-stationary.



Code
adf.test(log(y))



    Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test

data:  log(y)
Dickey-Fuller = -6.4215, Lag order = 5, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: stationary


Code
kpss.test(log(y))



    KPSS Test for Level Stationarity

data:  log(y)
KPSS Level = 2.8287, Truncation lag parameter = 4, p-value = 0.01


Code
z <- diff(diff(log(y)), lag = 12)
adf.test(z)



    Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test

data:  z
Dickey-Fuller = -5.1993, Lag order = 5, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: stationary


Code
kpss.test(z)



    KPSS Test for Level Stationarity

data:  z
KPSS Level = 0.084365, Truncation lag parameter = 4, p-value = 0.1


On log(y) the two tests disagree. adf.test() includes a linear trend term, so it only says “no unit root once you allow for a trend”. KPSS rejects a constant mean. After differencing, both agree the series is stationary. When tests conflict, trust the plots and the ACF as well, and say why in the write-up.


1.2.3 White noise


Code
set.seed(1)
wn <- rnorm(200)
plot.ts(wn, main = "White noise")









Code
acf(wn)









Code
Box.test(wn, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")



    Box-Ljung test

data:  wn
X-squared = 8.9624, df = 10, p-value = 0.5357


About 1 in 20 spikes will cross the blue lines just by chance. The Ljung-Box p-value is large, so we can’t reject white noise.


1.2.4 Benchmark forecasts and accuracy
Keep the last 2 years as a test set.


Code
train <- window(y, end = c(1958, 12))
test <- window(y, start = c(1959, 1))
h <- length(test)

f_mean <- meanf(train, h = h)
f_naive <- naive(train, h = h)
f_snaive <- snaive(train, h = h)
f_drift <- rwf(train, h = h, drift = TRUE)

plot(y, main = "Benchmark forecasts", xlim = c(1955, 1961))
lines(f_mean$mean, col = "blue")
lines(f_naive$mean, col = "red")
lines(f_snaive$mean, col = "darkgreen")
lines(f_drift$mean, col = "orange")
legend("topleft", c("mean", "naive", "seasonal naive", "drift"),
       col = c("blue", "red", "darkgreen", "orange"), lty = 1)











Code
acc <- rbind(
  mean = accuracy(f_mean, test)[2, ],
  naive = accuracy(f_naive, test)[2, ],
  snaive = accuracy(f_snaive, test)[2, ],
  drift = accuracy(f_drift, test)[2, ]
)
round(acc[, c("RMSE", "MAE", "MAPE", "MASE")], 2)


         RMSE    MAE  MAPE MASE
mean   219.44 206.34 44.23 7.22
naive  137.33 115.25 23.58 4.03
snaive  76.99  71.25 15.52 2.49
drift  115.70  91.62 18.41 3.21


Row 2 of accuracy() is the test set. Seasonal naive wins, because the series is so seasonal.


1.2.5 From first principles
Seasonal naive and RMSE by hand, to check that it matches snaive() and accuracy().


Code
my_snaive <- rep(tail(train, 12), length.out = h)
my_rmse <- sqrt(mean((test - my_snaive)^2))
my_rmse


[1] 76.99459


Code
accuracy(f_snaive, test)[2, "RMSE"]


[1] 76.99459




1.2.6 Time series cross validation
Rolling origin: forecast one step ahead from every point in the series, then average the errors. This gives a much better idea of accuracy than a single test set.


Code
e <- tsCV(y, snaive, h = 1)
sqrt(mean(e^2, na.rm = TRUE))


[1] 36.45315


Code
e2 <- tsCV(y, naive, h = 1)
sqrt(mean(e2^2, na.rm = TRUE))


[1] 33.82515




1.2.7 Key concepts
Why a random train/test split is wrong for time series. Time series observations depend on the ones before them, so a random split puts future values in the training set and past values in the test set. The model then gets to see information it would never have in practice, and its accuracy looks better than it really is. A test set should be the most recent part of the series, so the model is judged on data it could not have seen.
Why the ACF of a trending series decays slowly. If a series trends upward, each value is close to the values just before it, so it stays correlated with them across many lags. The autocorrelation at lag k stays high for a long stretch before it falls, which gives the slow decay. That slow decay is a sign the series is non-stationary, and differencing is usually needed before modelling.
The difference between a forecast, a goal and a plan. A forecast is a prediction of what will happen, based on the data and the model, whatever anyone wants to happen. A goal is what you would like to happen. A plan is what you will do to try to reach the goal. Keeping them separate matters because a forecast can show a goal is out of reach, and a plan should be built on the forecast, not on the goal.
Why a forecast is a distribution, and how the horizon should match the decision. A forecast is a random variable, so the honest answer is a range of likely values with probabilities attached, not one number. The uncertainty grows the further ahead you go, so the horizon should match the decision: a staff roster for next week needs a short-horizon forecast, while a five-year capacity plan needs a long one, and each comes with a wider interval.

text:
1.4 Diagnostic exercise (Section 7 of Intro to R)
In this section we run each of trhe example codes and explain what mistake was made in each.


Code
x <- 1:24

summ <- function(obj) {
  paste0("start=", paste(start(obj), collapse = "-"),
         "  end=", paste(end(obj), collapse = "-"),
         "  freq=", frequency(obj))
}

run_call <- function(label, expr) {
  res <- tryCatch({
    obj <- expr
    if (is.ts(obj)) summ(obj) else paste("returned", class(obj)[1])
  },
  error = function(e) paste("ERROR:", conditionMessage(e)),
  warning = function(w) paste("WARNING:", conditionMessage(w)))
  cat(label, ":", res, "\n")
}

run_call("Q1", ts(x, start = c(2023, 13), frequency = 12))


Q1 : start=2024-1  end=2025-12  freq=12 


Code
run_call("Q2", ts(x, start = 2023, frequency = 12))


Q2 : start=2023-1  end=2024-12  freq=12 


Code
run_call("Q3", ts(x, start = c(2023, 0), frequency = 12))


Q3 : start=2022-12  end=2024-11  freq=12 


Code
run_call("Q4", ts(x, start = c(2023, 2), frequency = 4))


Q4 : start=2023-2  end=2029-1  freq=4 


Code
run_call("Q5", ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12.5))


Q5 : start=2023  end=2024.84  freq=12.5 


Code
run_call("Q6", ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12, deltat = 1/12))


Q6 : start=2023-1  end=2024-12  freq=12 


Code
run_call("Q7", ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 365))


Q7 : start=2023-1  end=2023-24  freq=365 


Code
x_ts <- ts(x, start = c(2023, 1), frequency = 12)
run_call("Q8a", window(x_ts, start = c(2023, 13)))


Q8a : start=2024-1  end=2024-12  freq=12 


Code
run_call("Q8b", window(x_ts, start = c(2030, 1)))


Q8b : ERROR: 'start' cannot be after 'end' 


Code
run_call("Q9", decompose(ts(x, frequency = 1)))


Q9 : ERROR: time series has no or less than 2 periods 


Q1: Period 13 doesn’t exist, so R counts it as period 1 of the next year. The data shifts a year without a warning.
Q2: R reads a plain 2023 as the time 2023.0, which is January, so it works. c(2023, 1) is clearer because it names the period too.
Q3: Period 0 doesn’t exist, so R counts it as one period before January. The series starts in December 2022 instead of January 2023.
Q4: Frequency 4 means quarterly data, so 24 values cover six years, not two. c(2023, 2) is now the second quarter of 2023, not the second month.
Q5: R accepts 12.5 without an error, but a month can’t be half a period. The date labels break: the start shows only 2023, and the end shows 2024.84.
Q6: The two arguments agree, since 1/12 is the same as 12 periods per year, so R accepts the call. It should only fail when the two values disagree.
Q7: A frequency of 365 means daily data, so 24 values only cover 24 days. The end label reads 2023-24, which looks like a date but is really day 24 of the year.
Q8a: January 2024 is inside the series, so window() returns the data from that point on.
Q8b: The start, 2030, is after the end of the series, so window() stops with the error ‘start’ cannot be after ‘end’.
Q9: A frequency of 1 means there’s no seasonal cycle to extract. decompose() needs at least two full cycles, so it throws the error time series has no or less than 2 periods.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.5 Reflection
This first lecture and practice material was really interesting, but very hard to wrap my head around. There are so many functions and so many ways to format and view the data, with many different options for packages. It was very overwhelming and frustrating to figure out the differences and understand what goes where.
The theory from the slides was a lot of info to process too, and I’m not sure where it is going yet. We’ve already been introduced to forecasting and I’m still uncertain as to what we are forecasting from. I do not yet see or understand the models we will be dealing with, which I feel like would have helped understand why we do what we did in this section.
The main take aways I have gotten from this is first, how different time series data is to “regular” data. The number of new packages and functions we’ve been introduced to is really exciting. The second thing is how powerful some existing packages are for data visualisation. Some of these plots will be so helpful in future EDA for any projects I may do in any course, even when not using time series data.
I am very excited for the rest of this course and to get stuck into the modelling soon.

title: 2  ARIMA
text:
2.1 Overview
This section covers Part 1 - ARIMA models. The main ideas in ARIMA are as follows,

title: 2  ARIMA
text:
MA(q): \(y_t = \varepsilon_t + \theta_1 \varepsilon_{t-1} + \dots + \theta_q \varepsilon_{t-q}\). Always stationary. ACF cuts off after lag q.
AR(p): \(y_t = \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \dots + \phi_p y_{t-p} + \varepsilon_t\). Stationary if the roots of \(\phi(B)\) lie outside the unit circle (AR(1): \(|\phi| < 1\)). PACF cuts off after lag p.
ARMA(p, q): both ACF and PACF tail off.
ARIMA(p, d, q): ARMA on the d-times differenced series.
SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)\(_m\): adds seasonal AR/MA terms at lags m, 2m, … and D seasonal differences. Read the seasonal part from the ACF/PACF at lags m, 2m, 3m.
Box-Jenkins: (1) plot, transform and difference until stationary; (2) pick p, q, P, Q from the ACF/PACF; (3) estimate (maximum likelihood); (4) check that the residuals are white noise; (5) forecast.
Only compare AIC between models with the same differencing, because differencing changes the data the likelihood is computed on.
Prediction intervals get wider with the horizon. For a model with differencing they keep growing.

2.2 Worked Examples
This section shows how to identify AR and MA orders from the ACF and PACF, fits an AR(1) by hand and checks it against R, then builds and tests a seasonal ARIMA model for the air passenger data, and finally compares its forecasts with a seasonal naive benchmark.

2.2.1 Identification: what the ACF and PACF look like


Code
library(forecast)
library(readr)
library(here)
library(dplyr)

set.seed(10)
ar2 <- arima.sim(list(ar = c(0.6, 0.3)), n = 300)
ma1 <- arima.sim(list(ma = 0.7), n = 300)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
acf(ar2, main = "AR(2): ACF tails off")
pacf(ar2, main = "AR(2): PACF cuts off after 2")
acf(ma1, main = "MA(1): ACF cuts off after 1")
pacf(ma1, main = "MA(1): PACF tails off")









Code
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))




2.2.2 From first principles: fitting an AR(1)
Fit an AR(1) with mean \(\mu\) by minimising the conditional sum of squares:
\[ (y_t - \mu) = \phi (y_{t-1} - \mu) + \varepsilon_t \]


Code
set.seed(2)
x <- arima.sim(list(ar = 0.7), n = 200) + 5

css <- function(par, x) {
  mu <- par[1]
  phi <- par[2]
  n <- length(x)
  e <- (x[2:n] - mu) - phi * (x[1:(n-1)] - mu)
  sum(e^2)
}

fit_own <- optim(c(mean(x), 0), css, x = x)
fit_own$par


[1] 5.0012705 0.6351711


Code
# compare with R
arima(x, order = c(1, 0, 0), method = "CSS")

s.e.  0.0545     0.2071

sigma^2 estimated as 1.142:  part log likelihood = -297.04


The estimates match R’s arima() with method CSS. (R’s default is full maximum likelihood, which gives almost the same answer.)

2.2.7 The lag operator


Code
y <- c(3, 7, 4, 8, 5)
c(NA, y[1:(length(y)-1)]) # lag by hand


[1] NA  3  7  4  8


Code
#> [1] NA 3 7 4 8
dplyr::lag(y, n = 1) # same shift


[1] NA  3  7  4  8


Code
#> [1] NA 3 7 4 8
dplyr::lead(y, n = 1) # lead


[1]  7  4  8  5 NA


Code
#> [1] 7 4 8 5 NA




2.2.8 Key concepts
Reading p and q from the ACF and PACF. An AR(\(p\)) process has a PACF that cuts off after lag \(p\), while its ACF tails off. An MA(\(q\)) process has an ACF that cuts off after lag \(q\), while its PACF tails off. ARMA(\(p, q\)) has both tailing off. For seasonal orders, read \(P\) and \(Q\) from the same plots at lags \(m, 2m, 3m, \dots\). For monthly data, \(m = 12\), so a spike at lag 12 suggests a seasonal MA(1), \(Q = 1\).
Why take logs before differencing. The air passenger series has variance that grows with the level, so the log makes the variance roughly constant and turns multiplicative seasonality into additive. Differencing the log series, \(\nabla \log y_t = \log y_t - \log y_{t-1}\), gives approximately the percentage change in \(y_t\). lambda = 0 in Arima() fits on the log scale and back-transforms the forecasts.
Stationarity (AR) and invertibility (MA). An AR model is stationary when the roots of \(\phi(z) = 0\) lie outside the unit circle; for AR(1) this means \(|\phi| < 1\). An MA model is invertible when the roots of \(\theta(z) = 0\) lie outside the unit circle, so it can be rewritten as an infinite autoregression. Without invertibility, two different parameter values give the same ACF, so the estimates are not uniquely identified.
Why forecast intervals grow with \(h\). Future shocks \(\varepsilon_{t+j}\) are unknown, and each step adds another shock to the forecast error, so the forecast variance accumulates with the horizon \(h\). With differencing, the variance keeps growing rather than settling, since the level has a unit root. The intervals therefore widen roughly with \(\sqrt{h}\).
Why AIC can’t compare models with different \(d\). AIC compares likelihoods only when the models are fitted to the same data. Differencing once fits to \(n - 1\) values and differencing twice fits to \(n - 2\), so the likelihoods refer to different datasets. Choose \(d\) from plots and unit-root tests first, then use AIC to choose \(p\) and \(q\) within that \(d\). The same applies to the seasonal \(D\).

Code
## Question 8: coal production, AR(4)-type model by hand
c8   <- 146.1
phi8 <- c(0.891, -0.257, 0.392, -0.333)

# Last four observed values, most recent last: 1965 to 1968
y8 <- c(512, 534, 552, 545)

# Recursive forecasts for 1969 to 1971
# Each new forecast is fed back in as an input for the next one
for (h in 1:3) {
  n <- length(y8)
  new <- c8 + sum(phi8 * rev(y8[(n - 3):n]))
  y8 <- c(y8, new)
}
round(tail(y8, 3), 1)  # forecasts for 1969, 1970, 1971


[1] 528.7 515.6 499.5


Question 7 (US strikes). The first difference of the series has an ACF that cuts off after lag 1, which points to an MA(1) term once the series has been differenced once. The model can be written with the backshift operator as \((1 - B)y_t = (1 + \theta B)\varepsilon_t\), or equivalently \(y_t - y_{t-1} = \varepsilon_t + \theta\varepsilon_{t-1}\). Fitting it in R gives \(\hat\theta = -0.31\), which lies inside the unit circle so the model is invertible, and a Ljung-Box p-value of 0.78, so the residuals look like white noise and the model is satisfactory. The hand forecast of \(y_T + \hat\theta e_T = 4157.3\) matches R for all three years ahead, because the forecast is flat once future shocks are set to zero. The 95% prediction intervals widen across the horizon, from roughly 3030 to 5285 for the first year to roughly 2582 to 5733 for the third.
Question 8 (coal production). The model \(Y_t = c + \phi_1 Y_{t-1} + \phi_2 Y_{t-2} + \phi_3 Y_{t-3} + \phi_4 Y_{t-4} + e_t\) is an AR(4) model, so \(p = 4\), \(d = 0\) and \(q = 0\). It was chosen because it uses four lagged values of the series itself, with no differencing or moving-average terms. Using \(c = 146.1\) and the estimated coefficients, the forecasts are 528.7 for 1969, 515.6 for 1970 and 499.5 for 1971. The first forecast checks by hand as \(146.1 + 0.891(545) - 0.257(552) + 0.392(534) - 0.333(512) \approx 528.6\), with the small difference from rounding. Each later forecast uses the previous forecasts as inputs.

title: 2  ARIMA
text:
2.4 Reflection
It was really nice getting into some actual modelling. The theory made sense with plots illustrating things, but it made much more sense after coding it. My main confusion still lies around cross validation. I understand why it has to be different for Time Series data, but I the three methods are confusing. Walk-Forward and Expanding seem to be the same thing. Other theoretical concepts make sense when learning about them, like the different kinds of stationarity, but I often get mixed up when trying to remember what qualities align with which type.
The MA(q) and AR(p) formulas are really confusing to wrap my head around. Their recursive nature makes it so hard to visualise, that each prediction can be based on all past observations. Also it took me a long time to realise exactly what we are doing when we choose our models. I didn’t get why we want to transform our data to be white noise in the ACF plots, it seemed to defeat the points of modelling. I am still used to drawing a nice Linear Regression straight line through the data. I now understand, the modelling until residuals resemble white noise indicates we have modelled the pattern of the data as much as possible, and any further model complexitiy would overfit to noise in the data.
The adding of additional components, differencing and seasonality, were easy to understand, as by this stage I have resolved my confusions regarding ARMA models. In exercise 1 question 7b, it was so satisfying seeing the forecast plot of my full ARIMA model.
Overall, this was an extremely frustrating section, because my incorrect preconceptions and misunderstandings about where we were going with our modelling made understanding the modelling process very difficult. I felt like I thought I knew what was going on, but it never matched the results, until things clicked, and then everything fell into place. I also really enjoyed doing one of my projects on this section where I got to dive a lot deeper and get more practice (see {#sec-p1}).

title: 3  ARCH & GARCH
text:
3.1 Overview
This section covers covers Part 1 - ARCH and GARCH models (GARCH). The main concepts of GARCH are as follopws,
The full application is in Chapter 10.

title: 3  ARCH & GARCH
text:
Financial returns are roughly uncorrelated (so ARMA can’t predict them), but big moves follow big moves: volatility clustering. The squared returns are autocorrelated.
Model returns, not prices: \(r_t = 100 \times (\log P_t - \log P_{t-1})\).
Two equations: a mean model (\(r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t\)) and a variance model for \(\sigma_t^2 = \text{Var}(\varepsilon_t \mid \text{past})\), with \(\varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t\), \(z_t \sim\) iid(0, 1).
ARCH(1): \(\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2\). Gives clustering, but forgets too fast.
GARCH(1,1): \(\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2\). Needs \(\alpha_0 > 0\), \(\alpha_1, \beta_1 \ge 0\), \(\alpha_1 + \beta_1 < 1\).

\(\alpha_1\): how strongly volatility reacts to a shock.
\(\beta_1\): how long the reaction lasts.
Persistence \(= \alpha_1 + \beta_1\). Half life \(= \log(0.5) / \log(\alpha_1 + \beta_1)\).
Long run variance \(= \alpha_0 / (1 - \alpha_1 - \beta_1)\). Volatility forecasts revert to this level.

Testing for ARCH effects: Ljung-Box on squared returns, or Engle’s ARCH LM test (H0: no ARCH effects).
Diagnostics: standardised residuals \(z_t = \varepsilon_t / \sigma_t\) should have no autocorrelation in \(z_t\) or \(z_t^2\).
Returns have fat tails, so a Student t distribution for \(z_t\) often fits better than normal.
Asymmetry (GJR-GARCH): bad news raises volatility more than good news. Adds \(\gamma \, I(\varepsilon_{t-1} < 0) \, \varepsilon_{t-1}^2\).
Persistence very close to 1 can mean there is a structural break in the series.
GARCH doesn’t improve the point forecast. What it gives you is honest prediction intervals.

title: 3  ARCH & GARCH

3.2 Worked Examples
This worked example fits GARCH(1,1) to the DAX returns, checks for ARCH effects, interprets persistence and half-life, and compares the fit against a t distribution and a GJR-GARCH model.

The price is clearly not stationary. The returns have a constant mean of about 0, but quiet periods and wild periods.

Code

  variance.model = list(model = "gjrGARCH", garchOrder = c(1, 1)),

      Akaike        Bayes      Shibata Hannan-Quinn 
    2.688045     2.705886     2.688024     2.694620 


If gamma1 is positive and significant, negative returns increase volatility more than positive ones.


3.2.8 From first principles: GARCH(1,1) likelihood
With normal errors, the log-likelihood is \(\sum_t \log \phi(\varepsilon_t; 0, \sigma_t^2)\), where \(\sigma_t^2\) comes from the recursion. Start the recursion at the sample variance.


Code
garch_nll <- function(par, r) {
  mu <- par[1]
  omega <- par[2]
  alpha <- par[3]
  beta <- par[4]
  # constraints: return a huge value if they are broken
  if (omega <= 0 || alpha < 0 || beta < 0 || alpha + beta >= 1) return(1e10)

  n <- length(r)
  e <- r - mu
  s2 <- numeric(n)
  s2[1] <- var(r)
  for (t in 2:n) {
    s2[t] <- omega + alpha * e[t-1]^2 + beta * s2[t-1]
  }
  -sum(dnorm(e, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(s2), log = TRUE))
}

start <- c(mean(r), 0.1 * var(r), 0.1, 0.8)
fit_own <- optim(start, garch_nll, r = r)
round(fit_own$par, 4)


[1] 0.0654 0.0475 0.0684 0.8877


Code
round(coef(fit_norm), 4)


    mu  omega alpha1  beta1 
0.0654 0.0476 0.0685 0.8876 


My estimates are very close to rugarch’s normal GARCH(1,1). They differ a little because of how the first variance is initialised and the optimiser used.


3.2.9 Key concepts
Returns are almost unpredictable in direction, but their size is not. A big move today usually means a big move tomorrow, even if the direction is a coin toss. That is why the squared returns are correlated and the returns themselves are not.
Alpha is how hard volatility reacts to yesterday’s shock. Beta is how much of yesterday’s volatility carries over. Together they make persistence, which tells you how long a shock lingers. Persistence close to 1 means shocks fade slowly. Half-life is the number of days before a shock’s effect falls to half, so the higher the persistence, the longer the half-life.
The forecast goes back to the long-run level because each day’s forecast mixes the latest shock with the old forecast, and neither gets full weight. The shock’s influence shrinks each day, so the forecast drifts back to the average level the model settles on.
We check the squared standardised residuals because the model’s job is to capture changing volatility. If the squares still have autocorrelation, the volatility part of the model has missed the clustering, even if the residuals look fine on their own.
A t distribution fits returns better because real markets have more extreme days than a normal distribution allows. The t has fatter tails, so it gives those big days realistic probabilities. You can see this in the information criteria, where the t model usually scores better.

title: 3  ARCH & GARCH
text:
3.4 Reflection
GARCH felt like a natural extension of ARIMA models. Except it kind of wasn’t? At least not how I expected it to be. TI thought it was going to be as simple as adding some new variables to make error volatility dependent on time in addition to what was already modelled by ARIMA. While this is technically true, the application of GARCH means it is not so simple. GARCH focuses a lot on financial data, specifically on financial Returns data. This means that it is not as simple as adding a small extension to an ARIMA, but rather changing our whole approach and focus on to volatility. Because we focus on returns, the mean component (which I expected to be ARIMA) in my project just became a constant mean equation. The number of options on how to apply GARCH to a data set is staggering, and it is really difficult to know what approach to use. I ended up needing to trial and error, or work through things one step at a time, each time adding a new component, or trying a different model, and then checking which performed better. Once I understood the focus of GARCH is not to improve predictions, but rather to but model the uncertainity of those predictions, it started to make much more sense. For my GARCH Project 2, please see {#sec-p2}.

title: 4  Spectral Analysis
text:
4.1 Overview
This section covers Part 1 - Spectral Analysis. The main concepts are as follows,

title: 4  Spectral Analysis
text:
Period \(m\) = observations per cycle. Frequency \(f = 1/m\) = cycles per observation. Angular frequency \(\omega = 2\pi f\).
Careful: ts(..., frequency = 12) in R means the period (12 observations per year), not \(f\).
Nyquist frequency \(f = 0.5\): the fastest cycle you can see takes 2 observations. Faster cycles get aliased (they show up at a wrong, lower frequency). Monthly data can’t tell you anything about a weekly cycle.
The periodogram at the Fourier frequencies \(f_j = j/n\): \[ I(f_j) = \frac{1}{n} \left| \sum_{t=1}^n (y_t - \bar y) e^{-2\pi i f_j t} \right|^2 \] It splits the variance of the series over frequencies. A peak means a cycle with period \(1/f\).
Reading a periodogram, five steps:

Convert the peak to a period, with units (e.g. 12 months).
Check for harmonics (peaks at \(2f\), \(3f\) belong to the same cycle, just a non-sine shape).
Don’t trust one tall ordinate: the raw periodogram is very noisy.
Smooth it (spans) and keep only what survives.
Test the largest peak (Fisher’s g test, H0: white noise).

Spectra of familiar models: white noise is flat. AR(1) with \(\phi > 0\) has most power at low frequencies, with \(\phi < 0\) at high frequencies. Seasonal series have spikes at \(1/m\) and its harmonics.
Differencing removes low frequency power and adds high frequency power, so over-differencing is not harmless.
Use a periodogram when the question is about cycle lengths, or several cycles at once. Use the ACF/ARIMA when the question is about forecasting.

title: 4  Spectral Analysis
text:
4.2 Spectral analysis lab
I used the Spectral analysis lab and simplified it easier for me to understand.

4.2.1 A known cycle: period 24
We simulate a sine wave with period 24, then add noise.


Code
set.seed(100)
y_cyc <- 2 * sin(2 * pi * (1:240) / 24) + rnorm(240, 0, 0.4)
plot.ts(y_cyc, main = "Period 24 cycle plus noise")








Figure 4.1: A period-24 cycle buried in noise.





I expect the peak at a frequency of \(1/24 = 0.0417\) cycles per observation, which is a period of 24 observations.


Code
sp_cyc <- spec.pgram(y_cyc, taper = 0, detrend = FALSE, fast = FALSE, plot = FALSE)
plot(sp_cyc$freq, sp_cyc$spec, type = "h",
     xlab = "Frequency (cycles per observation)", ylab = "Spectrum",
     main = "Periodogram")
abline(v = 1 / 24, lty = 2)








Figure 4.2: Raw periodogram of the period-24 series. The dashed line marks \(f = 1/24\).







Code
peak_cyc <- sp_cyc$freq[which.max(sp_cyc$spec)]
c(peak_frequency = peak_cyc, peak_period = 1 / peak_cyc)


peak_frequency    peak_period 
    0.04166667    24.00000000 




4.2.2 Real data: the lynx cycle
The lynx series is very skewed, so we take logs and smooth the periodogram.


Code
ly <- log(lynx)
sp_ly <- spec.pgram(as.numeric(ly), spans = c(3, 3), plot = FALSE)
plot(sp_ly$freq, sp_ly$spec, type = "l",
     xlab = "Frequency (cycles per year)", ylab = "Spectrum",
     main = "Smoothed periodogram: log(lynx)")








Figure 4.3: Smoothed periodogram of log annual lynx trappings.







Code
peak_ly <- sp_ly$freq[which.max(sp_ly$spec)]
c(peak_frequency = peak_ly, period_years = 1 / peak_ly)


peak_frequency   period_years 
           0.1           10.0 




4.2.3 Testing the peak
Fisher’s g test asks whether the largest peak is bigger than white noise would produce. Here we apply it to the period-24 series.


Code
n <- length(y_cyc)
I <- Mod(fft(y_cyc - mean(y_cyc)))^2 / n
q <- floor((n - 1) / 2)
I <- I[2:(q + 1)]
g <- max(I) / sum(I)
p_value <- min(q * (1 - g)^(q - 1), 1)
c(g = g, p_value = p_value)


            g       p_value 
 9.370008e-01 2.495038e-140 


Here \(g\) is the largest ordinate as a share of the total, and the p-value is small when that share is too large for white noise.
The period-24 peak sits at \(f = 0.0417 = 1/24\), so the period is 24 observations, as built into the simulation. Fisher’s test gives \(g = 0.937\) with \(p = 2.5 \times 10^{-140}\) across \(q = 119\) ordinates, so white noise is rejected. The smoothed lynx spectrum peaks at \(f = 0.1\) cycles per year, a period of 10 years.

title: 4  Spectral Analysis
text:
4.3 Worked examples
In this worked example I take a series with a known cycle and a real dataset (the lynx series), and shows step by step how to find the peak in the periodogram, convert it to a period, and test whether it is real.

4.3.1 A known cycle: period 24 in noise


Code
set.seed(100)
n <- 240
t <- 1:n
y <- 2 * sin(2 * pi * t / 24) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.4)
plot.ts(y, main = "Period 24 cycle plus noise")











4.3.2 From first principles: the periodogram with fft()


Code
my_pgram <- function(y) {
  n <- length(y)
  y <- y - mean(y)
  I <- Mod(fft(y))^2 / n
  j <- 1:floor(n / 2)
  data.frame(freq = j / n, period = n / j, I = I[j + 1])
}

pg <- my_pgram(y)
pg[which.max(pg$I), ]







freq
period
I




10
0.0416667
24
234.5078






Code
plot(pg$freq, pg$I, type = "h", xlab = "frequency (cycles per observation)",
     ylab = "I(f)", main = "My periodogram")
abline(v = 1/24, col = "red", lty = 2)









Element \(k+1\) of fft(y) belongs to frequency \(k/n\), which is why the index is j + 1. The peak is at \(f = 0.0417 = 1/24\), so the period is 24 observations.
The same thing with R’s spec.pgram(). Turn off its defaults (taper, detrend, padding) to get the raw periodogram:


Code
sp <- spec.pgram(y, taper = 0, detrend = FALSE, fast = FALSE, plot = FALSE)
sp$freq[which.max(sp$spec)]


[1] 0.04166667


Code
1 / sp$freq[which.max(sp$spec)]


[1] 24




4.3.3 Testing the peak: Fisher’s g test
\(g\) = largest ordinate / sum of all ordinates. Under H0 (white noise), \(P(G > g) \approx q (1 - g)^{q-1}\), where \(q\) is the number of ordinates. This approximation is fine when the p-value is small.


Code
fisher_g <- function(y) {
  y <- y - mean(y)
  n <- length(y)
  I <- Mod(fft(y))^2 / n
  q <- floor((n - 1) / 2)
  I <- I[2:(q + 1)]
  g <- max(I) / sum(I)
  p <- q * (1 - g)^(q - 1)
  c(g = g, p_value = min(p, 1), period = n / which.max(I))
}

fisher_g(y)


            g       p_value        period 
 9.370008e-01 2.495038e-140  2.400000e+01 


Code
set.seed(2026)
fisher_g(rnorm(240))   # pure noise, so the p-value should be large


         g    p_value     period 
0.04863759 0.33141605 4.61538462 




4.3.4 Real data: the lynx cycle
Annual Canadian lynx trappings, 1821 to 1934. Use logs because the series is very skewed.


Code
ly <- log(lynx)
plot(ly, main = "log(lynx)")









Code
sp_raw <- spec.pgram(as.numeric(ly), taper = 0, detrend = FALSE, plot = FALSE)
sp_smooth <- spec.pgram(as.numeric(ly), spans = c(3, 3), plot = FALSE)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(sp_raw$freq, sp_raw$spec, type = "l", main = "raw", xlab = "freq (per year)", ylab = "spectrum")
plot(sp_smooth$freq, sp_smooth$spec, type = "l", main = "smoothed, spans = c(3,3)",
     xlab = "freq (per year)", ylab = "spectrum")









Code
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

peak <- sp_smooth$freq[which.max(sp_smooth$spec)]
c(freq = peak, period_years = 1 / peak)


        freq period_years 
         0.1         10.0 


Code
fisher_g(as.numeric(ly))


           g      p_value       period 
5.967384e-01 1.136230e-20 9.500000e+00 


There is a strong cycle of roughly 9 to 10 years, which survives smoothing and is highly significant. It is a cycle, not seasonality: it is caused by the predator-prey relationship, not the calendar.
Smoothing: too little and the spectrum stays noisy; too much and real peaks get flattened. Try a few spans.


4.3.5 Real data: monthly temperatures (seasonal)


Code
sp_t <- spec.pgram(as.numeric(nottem), spans = 3, plot = FALSE)
plot(sp_t$freq, sp_t$spec, type = "l", log = "y", main = "Nottingham monthly temps",
     xlab = "frequency (cycles per month)", ylab = "spectrum (log scale)")
abline(v = 1/12, col = "red", lty = 2)









The peak is at \(1/12\) cycles per month = a 12 month cycle.


4.3.6 Spectra of familiar models
The AR(1) spectrum is \(f(\omega) = \sigma^2 / (1 - 2\phi\cos(2\pi\omega) + \phi^2)\).


Code
f <- seq(0, 0.5, length.out = 200)
ar1_spec <- function(f, phi) 1 / (1 - 2 * phi * cos(2 * pi * f) + phi^2)

plot(f, ar1_spec(f, 0.8), type = "l", log = "y", ylim = c(0.2, 30),
     xlab = "frequency", ylab = "spectrum", main = "Theoretical spectra")
lines(f, ar1_spec(f, -0.8), col = "red")
abline(h = 1, col = "blue")
legend("top", c("AR(1) phi = 0.8", "AR(1) phi = -0.8", "white noise"),
       col = c("black", "red", "blue"), lty = 1)









Differencing multiplies the spectrum by \(|1 - e^{-2\pi i f}|^2 = 2 - 2\cos(2\pi f)\), which is 0 at \(f = 0\) and 4 at \(f = 0.5\). So differencing white noise creates high frequency power that wasn’t there before:


Code
plot(f, 2 - 2 * cos(2 * pi * f), type = "l", xlab = "frequency", ylab = "gain",
     main = "Effect of differencing on the spectrum")









Sampling once per observation, a cycle at \(f = 0.6\) is indistinguishable from one at \(f = 0.4\): over 20 observations the two sampled series differ by exactly zero. Anything above the Nyquist frequency of \(0.5\) is therefore aliased to a lower frequency.


4.3.7 Key concepts
Period, frequency and angular frequency: The period \(m\) is how many observations make one full cycle. The frequency is \(f = 1/m\), the number of cycles per observation. The angular frequency is \(\omega = 2\pi f\), which is the same cycle measured in radians. In ts(), the frequency argument is actually the period, so ts(x, frequency = 12) means 12 observations per year.
Aliasing: A cycle faster than the Nyquist frequency (\(f = 0.5\), two observations per cycle) cannot be seen properly. It shows up as a slower cycle at the wrong frequency. Monthly data, for example, cannot reveal a weekly cycle. Why smooth the periodogram: The raw periodogram is very noisy, so a single tall peak may be chance. Smoothing averages neighbouring ordinates, which makes genuine peaks easier to see. Too little smoothing leaves noise, and too much flattens real peaks.
Cycle versus seasonality: A cycle, such as the lynx series, has a period that is not tied to the calendar and comes from the system itself. Seasonality, such as monthly temperatures, repeats on a fixed calendar period, such as 12 months. When a periodogram beats the ACF: A periodogram is more useful when you want to know the length of one or more cycles, or when several cycles overlap. The ACF is more useful for forecasting with ARIMA-type models.

title: 4  Spectral Analysis
text:
4.4 Reflection
This section was so confusing. The Frequency domain just didn’t make sense to me. I could complete the Lab but I didn’t really understand what it was I was actually doing, or rather I didn’t see how it worked or how one would use it for modelling. I also got it a bit confused with harmonics in Time Series Regression ({Chapter 6}) but that is a variable describing the actual data, still in the time domain.
What really helped me to understand it was Peridogram in the following example. If I was to play a chord, three muscial notes on a piano, each one a frequency (a sinusoid). These three combine into one signal which gives us our time series in the time domain. That series is the sum of its parts, and it could be split back into those three sinusoids (the three piano notes), but from just the time domain plot of a seemingly random curve, you can’t see those orginal parts that make it up. The peridogram shows exactly which frequencies make up our time series, and we would be able to determine the exact three notes that make up our chord.
This helped me understand what we are doing in Spectral Analysis. We can determine a combination of sinusoids (or frequencies) that when added together can model our series. We can determine which sinusoids best model our data by idenfifying the frequencies on the Peridogram. The lab only have one frequency which made it harder to realise what was going on, but now that I’ve made the connection it seems as the harmonics in TSRegression.

title: 5  Exponential Smoothing
text:
5.1 Overview
This section covers Part 2 - Exponential Smoothing. I use ses(), holt(), hw() and ets() to fit models and read their output, including the parameter estimates. I choose between methods by looking at the time plot and, for the seasonal case, by comparing errors on a test set. I also write my own SES and Holt routines, minimise the sum of squared errors with optim(), and check the results against R’s functions. Finally, I construct prediction intervals from the normal formula and from bootstrapped residuals, and I compare the two.
The main ideas are as follows,

title: 5  Exponential Smoothing
text:
Simple exponential smoothing (SES): forecasts are weighted averages of past observations, with weights that decay exponentially: \(\alpha, \alpha(1-\alpha), \alpha(1-\alpha)^2, \dots\)

Smoothing equation: \(\ell_t = \alpha y_t + (1-\alpha)\ell_{t-1}\)
Forecast: \(\hat y_{t+h|t} = \ell_t\) (flat forecasts)
Estimate \(\alpha\) and \(\ell_0\) by minimising \(SSE = \sum (y_t - \hat y_{t|t-1})^2\).
Large \(\alpha\) = reacts fast, follows the last observation. Small \(\alpha\) = smooth, long memory.
SES is the optimal forecast for an ARIMA(0,1,1) and for a random walk plus noise.

Holt (double): adds a trend \(b_t\).

\(\ell_t = \alpha y_t + (1-\alpha)(\ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1})\)
\(b_t = \beta(\ell_t - \ell_{t-1}) + (1-\beta)b_{t-1}\)
\(\hat y_{t+h|t} = \ell_t + h b_t\). Damped trend multiplies the trend by \(\phi^h\) so forecasts flatten out.

Holt-Winters (triple): adds a seasonal component, additive (constant seasonal swings) or multiplicative (swings grow with the level).
ETS models (Error, Trend, Season) write these methods as state space models. That gives a likelihood, AIC for choosing between them, and proper prediction intervals.
SES on its own has no statistical model, so the intervals need a model assumption. Normal errors, ETS(A,N,N): \(\text{Var} = \sigma^2[1 + (h-1)\alpha^2]\). Or bootstrap the residuals.

title: 5  Exponential Smoothing
text:
5.2 Worked examples
This section shows how to fit simple exponential smoothing by hand and check it against ses(), then simulates data with a trend and fits Holt’s method both by hand and with holt(). It then compares Holt-Winters and ETS on the air passenger data using a test set, and finishes by checking which method forecasts best.

5.2.1 From first principles: SES
The same function as in the notes. Data: annual flow of the Nile, 1871 to 1970.


Code
library(forecast)
y <- Nile
plot(y, main = "Nile flow")









Code
ses_sse <- function(pars, y) {
  level0 <- pars[1]
  alpha <- pars[2]
  n <- length(y)
  yhat <- numeric(n + 1)
  level <- numeric(n)
  yhat[1] <- level0
  for (i in 1:n) {
    level[i] <- alpha * y[i] + (1 - alpha) * yhat[i]
    yhat[i + 1] <- level[i]
  }
  sum((y - yhat[1:n])^2)
}

fit <- optim(c(y[1], 0.5), ses_sse, y = y)
fit$par


[1] 1110.8426176    0.2457883


Compare with R:

fit_r$model

ses_run <- function(y, level0, alpha) {

title: 5  Exponential Smoothing
text:
5.3 Bootstrap prediction intervals for SES
Simulate many future paths by resampling the residuals, then take quantiles. This doesn’t assume normal errors.


Code
set.seed(1)
B <- 2000
H <- 5
sims <- matrix(NA, B, H)
for (b in 1:B) {
  lev <- fc
  for (j in 1:H) {
    ynew <- lev + sample(res, 1)
    sims[b, j] <- ynew
    lev <- a * ynew + (1 - a) * lev
  }
}
t(apply(sims, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975)))


         2.5%    97.5%
[1,] 483.5261 1061.913
[2,] 474.1460 1067.398
[3,] 469.4159 1093.799
[4,] 469.5431 1086.157
[5,] 459.3768 1092.167


These are similar to the normal intervals but not identical, because the bootstrap uses the actual residuals, which are a bit skewed. No normality assumption is needed.

5.3.1 From first principles: Holt
Simulate data from Holt’s model, so we know the true values (\(\alpha = 0.5\), \(\beta = 0.2\)). In error form, with one-step error \(e_t\): \(\ell_t = \ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1} + \alpha e_t\) and \(b_t = b_{t-1} + \alpha\beta e_t\).


Code
set.seed(3)
n <- 100
alpha <- 0.5
beta <- 0.2
level <- 10
trend <- 0.5
y2 <- numeric(n)
for (i in 1:n) {
  e <- rnorm(1, 0, 1)
  y2[i] <- level + trend + e
  new_level <- level + trend + alpha * e
  trend <- trend + alpha * beta * e
  level <- new_level
}
y2 <- ts(y2)
plot(y2, main = "Simulated data with a trend")











Code
holt_sse <- function(pars, y) {
  alpha <- pars[1]
  beta <- pars[2]
  level <- pars[3]
  trend <- pars[4]
  if (alpha <= 0 || alpha >= 1 || beta <= 0 || beta >= 1) return(1e15)
  sse <- 0
  for (i in 1:length(y)) {
    yhat <- level + trend
    sse <- sse + (y[i] - yhat)^2
    new_level <- alpha * y[i] + (1 - alpha) * (level + trend)
    trend <- beta * (new_level - level) + (1 - beta) * trend
    level <- new_level
  }
  sse
}

start <- c(0.5, 0.1, y2[1], y2[2] - y2[1])
fit_h <- optim(start, holt_sse, y = y2, control = list(maxit = 5000))
fit_h$par


[1] 0.4869008 0.2436101 9.3305499 0.3561158


The estimates are close to the true 0.5 and 0.2.

fit_hr$model

R’s holt() reports \(\beta\) in a different form: R’s beta = \(\alpha \times\) the \(\beta\) in our notes. So fit_h$par[1] * fit_h$par[2] should equal R’s beta, and it does. \(\alpha\), \(\ell_0\) and \(b_0\) match directly.

5.3.2 Choosing a method








What the data look like
Method
R




No trend, no seasonality
Simple exponential smoothing
ses()


Trend
Holt’s linear method

Trend that should flatten out in the long run
Damped trend

Holt-Winters additive

Trend and seasonal swings that grow with the level
Holt-Winters multiplicative

Look at the time plot first, then confirm with a test set, or with AIC through ets(), which picks between these as models. Damped trends often forecast better beyond a few steps, because straight-line trends rarely last.

5.4.3 Question 3


Code
# Question 1 function modified to return the sum of squared one-step errors
ses_sse <- function(pars, y) {
  l <- pars[1]
  alpha <- pars[2]
  sse <- 0
  for (i in seq_along(y)) {
    e <- y[i] - l
    sse <- sse + e^2
    l <- l + alpha * e   # same as alpha * y[i] + (1 - alpha) * l
  }
  sse
}

oil_sub <- window(oil, start = 1996, end = 2013)

fit_optim <- optim(c(oil_sub[1], 0.5), ses_sse, y = oil_sub,
                   method = "L-BFGS-B",
                   lower = c(-Inf, 0), upper = c(Inf, 1))
fit_sub <- ses(oil_sub, h = 1)

rbind(optim = fit_optim$par,
      ses = c(fit_sub$model$par["l"], fit_sub$model$par["alpha"]))

ses   446.5868 0.8338901

title: 5  Exponential Smoothing
text:
5.5 Reflection
I really enjoyed this section. Understanding the math was hard but the idea was simple, our data is a single random reaslisation of an underlying process. It was really cool to make forecasts that when compared to the actual data fit really nicely. The smoothed line also feels like a nice “average” in Figure 5.3. ARIMA usually always looked similar to a naive model, but this feels like we’ve really identified the underlying trend. It was also nice to have a previous understanding of trend and seasonality. The difference between confidence and prediction intervals was also interesting. A confidence interval is an interval estimate for a parameter or the mean. It describes uncertainty in the estimate. A prediction interval is an interval for a future observation. It includes the noise in that observation, so it is wider.
Writing my own SES and Holt routines showed me where R’s numbers come from. The recursion that confused me at first became clear once I ran it on the Nile data, each fitted value is the previous level, and the forecast is the last level. Minimising my own SSE with optim() on the oil data from 1996 to 2013 gave \(\hat\alpha = 0.834\) and \(\hat\ell_0 = 446.58\), which match ses() to the printed precision. That check mattered most, because it showed the optimiser and R agree.
Two results surprised me. For the full oil series, \(\hat\alpha = 0.9999\), so the forecast is flat at the last level for all four years. And my own 95% interval for the oil forecast is narrower than R’s, which comes from using a different variance estimate, not from a different forecast. For the marathon data, my normal interval matches R’s to within 0.0002, so the only difference was the rounding of 1.96.
The smoothing parameter \(\alpha\) controls how quickly the level reacts to new data. When \(\alpha\) is close to 1, the level almost follows the last observation and the method has a short memory. When \(\alpha\) is close to 0, the level changes slowly and averages over a long history.
The level \(\ell_t\) is the smoothed estimate of the current state. The fitted value \(\hat y_{t|t-1} = \ell_{t-1}\) is the one-step-ahead prediction made before \(y_t\) is seen, and the forecast \(\hat y_{t+h|t} = \ell_t\) is the prediction \(h\) steps ahead. SES forecasts are flat because the method assumes no trend and no seasonality, so every future value is the current level.
Holt-Winters adds seasonality. Additive seasonality adds a fixed seasonal amount, which suits swings of constant size. Multiplicative seasonality multiplies the level by a seasonal factor, which suits swings that grow with the level.
ETS writes each method as a state space model with an explicit error distribution. That gives a likelihood, so models can be compared with AIC, and the prediction intervals come from the model.
A confidence interval describes uncertainty in a parameter or the mean. A prediction interval describes uncertainty in a future observation, which also includes the noise term.

title: 6  Time Series Regression
text:
6.1 Overview
This section covers Part 2, regression for time series. I fit regression with ARMA errors using arima() and gls(), and I minimise the sum of squared errors myself with optim() to check the result against arima(). I fit ARMAX, VAR and GARMA models in R, use harmonic terms and dummy variables for seasonality and interventions, and fit a Poisson model with a spline trend to counts. I also show why regression on autocorrelated series can mislead, using two random walks, and I finish with forecasts from a regression with AR(1) errors.
The key concepts in this section are as follows,

title: 6  Time Series Regression
text:
Ordinary regression assumes independent errors. In time series the errors are usually autocorrelated, so the standard errors and p-values from lm() are wrong (usually too small), even if the coefficients are fine.
Regression with ARMA errors: \(y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_t + \eta_t\), where \(\eta_t\) follows an ARMA model. Fit with arima(y, order, xreg = x), with gls(), or by minimising the SSE yourself.
ARMAX is different: lagged \(y\) goes in as a predictor (\(y_t = \beta x_t + \phi y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t\)), which changes what \(\beta\) means.
Harmonic regression: model seasonality with sine and cosine terms \[ \sin(2\pi k t / m), \quad \cos(2\pi k t / m), \quad k = 1, 2, \dots \] Fewer parameters than one dummy per month, and it works with long periods (e.g. 365.25).
Indicator (dummy) variables: for seasons (one per month minus one), or for interventions such as a new law or a lockdown.
Non-normal response: for counts use a GLM, e.g. Poisson with a log link. Check for overdispersion (residual deviance much bigger than its df → quasipoisson or negative binomial).
Splines: a flexible smooth trend instead of a straight line, e.g. ns(t, df = 4).
VAR(p): several series that all depend on each other’s past values. For two series, \(y_t = \alpha_1 + b_{11} y_{t-1} + b_{12} z_{t-1} + e_t\) and \(z_t = \alpha_2 + b_{21} y_{t-1} + b_{22} z_{t-1} + w_t\). Each equation can be fitted by least squares. Impulse response functions show how a shock in one series moves the others over time.
GARMA: regression with ARMA-type terms for non-normal responses (e.g. counts). The ARMA terms go inside the linear predictor: \(g(\mu_t) = x_t'\beta + \sum \phi_k (g(y_{t-k}) - x_{t-k}'\beta) + \sum \theta_k (g(y_{t-k}) - \eta_{t-k})\). Fitted by maximum likelihood.
Spurious regression: regressing one random walk on another, unrelated one often gives a “highly significant” slope. Difference first, or model the errors.
Always check the residual ACF at the end.

title: 6  Time Series Regression
text:
6.2 Worked examples
This section starts with harmonic regression on the Nottingham temperatures and compares it with month dummies using AIC. It then fits regression with AR(1) errors to the beaver data, both with arima() and by minimising the SSE by hand, and compares the standard errors with OLS. Next, a Poisson model with a law dummy, a spline trend and harmonic terms is fitted to the Seatbelts data and corrected for overdispersion. The section then contrasts ARMAX with regression on AR(1) errors, forecasts with a regressor, shows spurious regression on random walks, fits a VAR(1) to simulated data, and ends with a GARMA model for polio counts, including a Poisson GARMA(1, 0) likelihood written from first principles.

6.2.1 Harmonic regression vs month dummies
Monthly average temperature at Nottingham, 1920 to 1939.


Code
y <- nottem
t <- 1:length(y)
plot(y, main = "Nottingham monthly temperature")









Code

m2 <- lm(y ~ sin(2*pi*t/12) + cos(2*pi*t/12) + sin(2*pi*2*t/12) + cos(2*pi*2*t/12))

# one dummy per month

m3 <- lm(y ~ month)

c(harm1 = AIC(m1), harm2 = AIC(m2), dummies = AIC(m3))

6.2.2 Regression with AR(1) errors
beaver2 (built into R): body temperature of a beaver every 10 minutes, and whether it was active (1) or not (0).

The PACF cuts off after lag 1, so try AR(1) errors:
\[ \text{temp}_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{activ}_t + \eta_t, \qquad \eta_t = \phi \eta_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t \]


Code
fit_ar <- arima(b$temp, order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = b$activ)
fit_ar



Call:
arima(x = b$temp, order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = b$activ)

Coefficients:
         ar1  intercept  b$activ
      0.8733    37.1920   0.6139
s.e.  0.0684     0.1187   0.1381

sigma^2 estimated as 0.01518:  log likelihood = 66.78,  aic = -125.55


Code

6.2.3 From first principles: minimise the SSE
Substitute \(\eta_t = y_t - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_t\) into the AR(1) equation, so \(\varepsilon_t = \eta_t - \phi\,\eta_{t-1}\), and minimise \(\sum \varepsilon_t^2\).


Code
sse_ar1 <- function(par, y, x) {
  b0 <- par[1]
  b1 <- par[2]
  phi <- par[3]
  eta <- y - b0 - b1 * x
  n <- length(y)
  e <- eta[2:n] - phi * eta[1:(n-1)]
  sum(e^2)
}

start <- c(coef(ols), 0.5)
fit_own <- optim(start, sse_ar1, y = b$temp, x = b$activ, control = list(maxit = 2000))
round(fit_own$par, 4)


(Intercept)       activ             
    37.2844      0.5842      0.8255 


Code
round(coef(fit_ar), 4)


      ar1 intercept   b$activ 
   0.8733   37.1920    0.6139 


Close to arima(), but not identical: arima() uses full maximum likelihood, while this conditional SSE drops the first observation. Both say the same thing. Compare the standard error of the activity effect:

  ar1_se = sqrt(fit_ar$var.coef["b$activ", "b$activ"]))

0.04389429 0.13808580 


With AR(1) errors the standard error is much bigger. OLS was too confident.

6.2.5 ARMAX: lagged y as a predictor
Back to the beaver data, but now with the previous temperature as a predictor:
\[ \text{temp}_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{activ}_t + \phi\, \text{temp}_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t \]


Code

round(coef(armax), 4)


(Intercept)       activ    temp_lag

Code

coef(armax)["activ"] / (1 - coef(armax)["temp_lag"])

0.736709 


The activity coefficient is much smaller here than in the AR-errors model. That’s because in ARMAX it’s only the immediate effect of activity, with yesterday’s temperature held fixed. The effect builds up over time, and the long run effect is \(\beta_1 / (1 - \phi)\), which is close to the AR-errors estimate. In regression with ARMA errors, \(\beta_1\) is the effect on the mean directly. That’s the main difference between the two models.

To forecast you need future values of the regressor. Here: assume the beaver stays active for the next hour (6 time steps).

6.2.9 GARMA: counts with autocorrelation
Monthly polio cases in the US, 1970 to 1983. These are counts, so a normal model doesn’t fit, and the counts are autocorrelated, so a plain GLM doesn’t either.


Code
library(gamlss.data)
data(polio, package = "gamlss.data")
df <- data.frame(pol = as.numeric(polio), mnth = 0:167)
plot(df$pol, type = "h", xlab = "month", ylab = "cases", main = "Polio cases")








Figure 6.1: Monthly polio cases in the United States, 1970 to 1983.







6.2.10 From first principles: a Poisson GARMA(1, 0)
With a log link and one AR term, the linear predictor is
\[ \eta_t = x_t'\beta + \phi\,(\log y^*_{t-1} - x_{t-1}'\beta), \qquad y^*_{t-1} = \max(y_{t-1}, 0.1) \]
(the max avoids \(\log 0\)). Then \(y_t \sim \text{Poisson}(e^{\eta_t})\), and we maximise the log-likelihood.


Code
y <- df$pol
mnth <- df$mnth
X <- cbind(1, cos(2*pi*mnth/12), sin(2*pi*mnth/12), cos(4*pi*mnth/12), sin(4*pi*mnth/12))

garma_nll <- function(par, y, X) {
  k <- ncol(X)
  beta <- par[1:k]
  phi <- par[k + 1]
  xb <- as.numeric(X %*% beta)
  ystar <- pmax(y, 0.1)
  n <- length(y)
  eta <- xb[2:n] + phi * (log(ystar[1:(n-1)]) - xb[1:(n-1)])
  -sum(dpois(y[2:n], exp(eta), log = TRUE))
}

m_glm <- glm(y ~ X - 1, family = poisson)       # no autocorrelation, for starting values
fit_g <- optim(c(coef(m_glm), 0), garma_nll, y = y, X = X, method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE)

round(cbind(estimate = fit_g$par, se = sqrt(diag(solve(fit_g$hessian)))), 3)


   estimate    se
X1    0.343 0.102
X2   -0.141 0.116
X3   -0.528 0.138
X4    0.207 0.110
X5   -0.416 0.110
      0.228 0.051


Code

m_glm2 <- glm(y[-1] ~ X[-1, ] - 1, family = poisson)
c(glm = AIC(m_glm2), garma = 2 * fit_g$value + 2 * 6)

565.2906 545.8281 


\(\hat\phi\) is clearly positive and the AIC drops a lot, so last month’s count helps predict this month’s, beyond the seasonal pattern.

title: 6  Time Series Regression
text:
6.3 Reflection
I was really excited for this section, as I’ve always wondered how to account for time in linear regression models. I have a background in property management, and while there are many variables that determine the value of a property, a major one is time. The whole industry is built on the assumption that property values rise over time.
I explain further in my Time Series Regression Project 3 {Chapter 11}, but my main struggle with this was assuming that the only way time was added to for example a property valuation model, was through the ARMA error terms. It also doesn’t apply to valuing a single property based off sales of past other properties, but rather it would be based on regular valuations of the same property. It took some time, but I eventually figured out how time series regression can incorporate time in its variables, and the ARMA errors. This was similar to the issues I had with GARCH {Chapter 3}, where I had an expectation of this new approach would work, but initially failed to identify the unique circumstances in which GARCH would be applicable, specifically to financial returns for GARCH. For time series regression, it obviously has a focus on time series data, which while I am used to now from ARIMA models, I am not used to this kind of data in a Regression context, and it took me a while to realise that these varibles that had time contextual information where not a part of the ARMA errors. I thought that the ARMA errors were the new addition to regression models, which they are, but in doing so I assumed these new kinds of variables were a part of that new addition of time dependent errors.
Two harmonics gave a lower AIC than twelve month dummies (1091.866 against 1097.645) with five parameters instead of twelve. OLS standard errors were too small for the beaver data: 0.0439 under OLS against 0.1381 with AR(1) errors. For the seatbelt counts, the overdispersion ratio was 2.4862, so I used quasipoisson, and the law corresponds to a fall of about 17.8%. ARMAX’s long-run effect of 0.7367 is well above the AR-errors estimate of 0.6139, so the two models differ. The polio GARMA gives phi = 0.228, and AIC falls from 565.29 to 545.83.
Autocorrelated errors leave the coefficients from lm() usable, but its standard errors come out too narrow, so effects look firmer than they are. With ARMA errors the autocorrelation sits in the error term and the slope is the direct effect on the mean. In ARMAX the lagged response is a predictor, so the slope is only the immediate effect, and the long-run effect is that slope divided by one minus the lag coefficient. Harmonic terms, sine and cosine pairs at multiples of the seasonal frequency, describe a seasonal pattern with far fewer parameters than dummies, and the example picks the number of harmonics by AIC.
A Poisson coefficient sits on the log scale, and the example converts the seatbelt-law coefficient into a percentage change using the exponential, holding trend and season fixed. Overdispersion means the residual deviance is much bigger than its degrees of freedom, and I check it with that ratio, which should be close to one. For the seatbelt model the ratio is above one, so I used quasipoisson, which keeps the estimates but widens the standard errors.
A VAR models each series from past values of both series, and each equation is an ordinary least squares regression on lagged values. An impulse response shows how a one-unit shock to one series moves the other over later steps; in the simulation, z responds upward to a shock to y and the effect fades. A plain GLM does not fit the autocorrelated polio counts, so GARMA adds ARMA-type terms to the linear predictor and is fitted by maximum likelihood. Two independent random walks can look strongly related because both wander, which leaves autocorrelated residuals and standard errors far too small. For forecasting, a regression needs future values of the regressor, which the example assumes for the next stretch of steps, and the prediction interval does not include uncertainty about them.

title: 7  State Space Models
text:
7.1 Overview
This section covers Part 2 - State Space models. A state space model splits a time series into a hidden state that changes over time and observations that are a noisy view of that state. I write out the local level model, the linear growth model and the basic structural model, and I show how the Kalman filter updates the state as each observation arrives. I estimate the variances V and W by maximum likelihood with dlm, and I check the filtered and smoothed estimates against the package. I also show how ARIMA can be written in state space form. My own Kalman filter code is in Project 4 (Chapter 12), so this section uses dlm for the fitting.
The key concepts in this section are as follows,

title: 7  State Space Models
text:
A state space model has a hidden state \(\theta_t\) and observations \(y_t\):

Observation equation: \(y_t = F_t \theta_t + v_t\), \(v_t \sim N(0, V)\)
System (state) equation: \(\theta_t = G_t \theta_{t-1} + w_t\), \(w_t \sim N(0, W)\)
Starting value: \(\theta_0 \sim N(m_0, C_0)\)

Local level model (random walk plus noise): \(F = G = 1\). The level wanders slowly and we see it with noise. \(V\) = observation noise, \(W\) = how much the level moves.
The Kalman filter, for each time t:

Predict the state: \(a_t = G m_{t-1}\), \(R_t = G C_{t-1} G' + W\)
Predict y: \(f_t = F a_t\), \(Q_t = F R_t F' + V\)
Update with the new observation: \(e_t = y_t - f_t\), Kalman gain \(K_t = R_t F' Q_t^{-1}\)
\(m_t = a_t + K_t e_t\), \(C_t = R_t - K_t F R_t\)

The gain decides how much to trust the new observation vs the prediction. Big \(W/V\) → big gain → follow the data.
Filtered \(E(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})\) uses data up to t. Smoothed \(E(\theta_t \mid y_{1:n})\) uses all the data, so it’s better for looking back. Predicted \(E(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1})\).
Missing values and forecasts: no observation → skip the update (\(K_t = 0\)), so the variance just grows. To forecast, add NAs to the end of y.
Estimation: the likelihood comes from the one-step prediction errors, \(\log L = \sum_t \log N(y_t; f_t, Q_t)\). Maximise over \(V\) and \(W\), on the log scale so they stay positive.
Linear growth (local linear trend): \(y_t = \mu_t + v_t\), \(\mu_t = \mu_{t-1} + \beta_{t-1} + w_t\), \(\beta_t = \beta_{t-1} + \gamma_t\). The level moves with a slope that itself wanders.
Basic structural model (BSM): linear growth plus a seasonal component \(s_t = -\sum_{j=1}^{S-1} s_{t-j} + \delta_t\) (seasonal effects sum to about 0 over a year). Level, trend, season and noise are all separate parts of the state. These are structural time series models.
Kalman smoother: runs backwards from the end, \(s_t = m_t + C_t G' R_{t+1}^{-1}(s_{t+1} - a_{t+1})\), \(S_t = C_t - C_t G' R_{t+1}^{-1}(R_{t+1} - S_{t+1}) R_{t+1}^{-1} G C_t\).
The Bayesian approach gives full uncertainty for \(V\) and \(W\) too, and handles missing data naturally.

title: 7  State Space Models
text:
7.2 Worked examples
This section starts with a local level model fitted to the Nile flows with dlm. It estimates V and W by maximum likelihood, plots the filtered and smoothed level, checks the standardised residuals, and forecasts ten years ahead with prediction limits. Next, the basic structural model is fitted to UK gas consumption on the log scale, with seasonal effects that are allowed to change over time. The section then writes an AR(2) model in state space form and checks the Kalman filter likelihood against arima().

7.2.1 Local level model: Nile


Code
library(dlm)
y <- as.numeric(Nile)
n <- length(y)




Code
build <- function(parm) dlmModPoly(order = 1, dV = exp(parm[1]), dW = exp(parm[2]))
fit_dlm <- dlmMLE(y, parm = c(0, 0), build = build)
fit_dlm$convergence


[1] 0


Code
exp(fit_dlm$par)


[1] 15099.803  1468.432


The maximum likelihood fit converged (convergence code 0), giving V = 15099.803 and W = 1468.432 (see chk-ssm-nile). The notes used these values as fixed illustrations, so this is the first time I’ve estimated them from the data.


Code
mod <- build(fit_dlm$par)
filt <- dlmFilter(y, mod)
smooth <- dlmSmooth(filt)




Code
plot(1871:1970, y, type = "l", col = "grey", xlab = "year", ylab = "flow", main = "Nile: local level model")
lines(1871:1970, dropFirst(filt$m), col = "blue")
lines(1871:1970, dropFirst(smooth$s), col = "red")
legend("topright", c("data", "filtered", "smoothed"), col = c("grey", "blue", "red"), lty = 1)








Figure 7.1: Nile flow with the filtered and smoothed local level from dlm.







Code

fc_se <- sqrt(unlist(fc_dlm$Q))
plot(1871:1970, y, type = "l", xlim = c(1871, 1980), xlab = "year", ylab = "flow", main = "Nile: 10-year forecast")

lines(1971:1980, fc_dlm$f - 1.96 * fc_se, col = "purple", lty = 2)
lines(1971:1980, fc_dlm$f + 1.96 * fc_se, col = "purple", lty = 2)








Figure 7.2: Ten-year forecast from the local level model, with 95% prediction limits.





The forecast is flat at 798.3885 for all ten years, because a local level model has no trend. The standard error grows from 143.5261 in the first year to 183.8903 in the tenth, because the level variance is added at each step (see chk-ssm-nile).

7.2.2 Linear growth and the basic structural model: UK gas

Code
build_bsm <- function(p) {
  dlmModPoly(order = 2, dV = exp(p[1]), dW = c(exp(p[2]), exp(p[3]))) +
    dlmModSeas(frequency = 4, dV = 0, dW = c(exp(p[4]), 0, 0))
}
fit_bsm <- dlmMLE(lg, parm = rep(-5, 4), build = build_bsm)

0.0000000000 0.0000918821 0.0037839289 0.0019500240

The level variance is effectively zero, so most of the movement sits in the seasonal and observation terms. StructTS() also gives a level variance of 0 and a slope variance of 0.0000918821 on the same log scale. Its seasonal and observation variances (0.0037839289 and 0.0019500240) are a little larger than the dlm values (see chk-ssm-gas).

title: 7  State Space Models
text:
7.3 Reflection
This was a nice section. It felt intuitive, building on exponential smoothing with an underlying state. The struggle was mostly with understanding the maths. The updating after seeing new observations has a similar feel to Bayes, which seems very logical to me.
In ARIMA the model describes the autocorrelation of what I observe. Here the model describes a hidden state that drives what I observe, and the Kalman filter updates my estimate of that state each time a new observation arrives. The part that took me longest was seeing that the one-dimensional case uses the same formulas as the matrix notation on the slides, with the state simply being size one.
Project 4 (Chapter 12) is where most of the difficulty was. My first simulation drew the state twice in each step, so the observations and the state did not match. I only noticed when the plots disagreed. Then I passed rnorm() the variance when it needs the standard deviation, so I had to take square roots. In the filter I first used a random draw in place of the variance \(W\), which gave a negative \(R_t\), and I also used all of \(F_t\) where I needed only the current value. Each mistake was small, but each one gave a plausible-looking result until I checked it.
The estimation step taught me the most. The slides do not show how \(V\) and \(W\) are estimated, so I had to work out for myself that the one-step prediction errors give the likelihood, and why the parameters go on the log scale so that they stay positive. My estimates were \(\hat{V} = 1.5761\) and \(\hat{W} = 1.3909\), against true values of \(V = 2\) and \(W = 1\). The total noise is about right, but some of it has been assigned to the wrong equation. The slides warn that the variances can be hard to tell apart, and I think that is what I saw.
The filter itself did what it should. The filtered state had a mean squared error of 0.88 against the true state, compared with 2.06 for the raw observations, so it tracks the state better than the data do. Forecasts decay towards zero within two or three steps, because the sign-flipping \(G_t\) multiplies the state by about one half each time. The prediction intervals looked too wide at first, and I thought they were useless. Checking coverage changed my mind, as 94% of the one-step 95% intervals contained the observation, so they are honest about how uncertain the state is.
The bit that confused me most was tracking \(V\) and \(W\). I kept having to work out how to rewrite the formulas each time they appeared in later steps, but I now understand what they mean. If \(W\) is large relative to \(V\), the filter follows the data more closely. If the ratio is reversed, the filter is smoother. A filter has access only to the observations up to the current time. Prediction uses all the prior data to forecast each point one step ahead. Smoothing uses the whole series, starting at the end and working backwards.

title: 8  Hidden Markov models
text:
8.1 Overview
This section covers Part 2 - hidden Markov models (HMMs). They are the discrete-state case of the state space models in Chapter 7: the hidden state follows a first-order Markov chain and can take only a finite number of values. Because the state is discrete, the Kalman filter does not apply. Instead, the likelihood is found by summing over the state sequence with the forward algorithm. I write out that likelihood, fit one-, two- and three-state Poisson models to the discoveries counts, and compare them by AIC and BIC. I then decode the most likely states, check the two-state fit with depmixS4, and forecast the next state and count.
The key concepts in this section are as follows,

title: 8  Hidden Markov models
text:
A hidden Markov model has a hidden state \(C_t \in \{1, \dots, m\}\) that follows a Markov chain, and observations \(X_t\) whose distribution depends on the current state.

Transition probability matrix \(\Gamma\), with \(\gamma_{ij} = P(C_{t+1} = j \mid C_t = i)\). Rows sum to 1.
Initial distribution \(\delta\).
State-dependent distributions \(p_i(x)\), e.g. Poisson(\(\lambda_i\)) for counts.

Likelihood: \(L_T = \delta P(x_1) \Gamma P(x_2) \Gamma \cdots \Gamma P(x_T) \mathbf{1}'\), where \(P(x)\) is a diagonal matrix holding \(p_1(x), \dots, p_m(x)\). It is computed with the forward algorithm, rescaling at each step so that it does not underflow.
Fitting: maximise the likelihood numerically, with parameters transformed so that they are unconstrained: \(\log \lambda_i\), and the off-diagonal entries of \(\Gamma\) on a log scale, with each row then divided by its sum.
Choosing m: compare AIC and BIC. BIC penalises extra states more heavily.
Decoding: local decoding gives the most likely state at each time separately, from the posterior probabilities. Global decoding gives the most likely whole sequence, found with the Viterbi algorithm.
Starting values matter, because the likelihood can have several local maxima, so I try more than one.
If the rows of \(\Gamma\) are identical, the states are independent and the HMM reduces to an independent mixture model.

title: 8  Hidden Markov models
text:
8.2 Worked examples
This section fits Poisson hidden Markov models to the annual counts of great discoveries from 1860 to 1959, which are built into R. I use these counts throughout, including for Question 8 of the tutorial, because the earthquake file was not available. The likelihood is computed with the forward algorithm, the models are fitted by maximum likelihood, and the states are decoded and forecast.

8.2.1 Data: great discoveries per year


Code
x <- as.numeric(discoveries)
n <- length(x)
years <- as.numeric(time(discoveries))




Code
plot(years, x, type = "h", xlab = "year", ylab = "count", main = "")








Figure 8.1: Number of great discoveries per year, 1860 to 1959.







Code
c(mean = mean(x), var = var(x))


    mean      var 
3.100000 5.080808 


The variance (5.08) is larger than the mean (3.10), so a single Poisson does not fit well. The counts may switch between a low and a high rate, which is what a hidden Markov model allows for.


8.2.2 The DAG
The dependence structure of an HMM can be drawn as a directed acyclic graph. Arrows show what depends on what:
C1 ---> C2 ---> C3 ---> ... ---> CT      hidden states: a Markov chain
|       |       |                |
v       v       v                v
X1      X2      X3      ...      XT      observations
Two things can be read off the graph. The state \(C_t\) depends only on \(C_{t-1}\) (the Markov property), and given the states, the observations are independent, with \(X_t\) depending only on \(C_t\). The joint distribution is the product of each node given its parents:
\[ p(c_{1:T}, x_{1:T}) = \delta_{c_1} \prod_{t=2}^{T} \gamma_{c_{t-1} c_t} \prod_{t=1}^{T} p_{c_t}(x_t) \]
Summing this over all possible state sequences gives the likelihood. The matrix product \(\delta P(x_1)\Gamma P(x_2)\cdots\) does that sum efficiently.


8.2.3 From first principles: the likelihood
I unpack the unconstrained parameter vector into \(\lambda\), \(\Gamma\) and the stationary \(\delta\), then compute the likelihood with the forward algorithm, scaled at every step as in the notes (the pois2.hmm.ll function). unpack is a helper for hmm_nll, and both are needed for Question 8.


Code
unpack <- function(par, m) {
  lambda <- exp(par[1:m])
  Gamma <- matrix(1, m, m)
  k <- m + 1
  for (i in 1:m) {
    for (j in 1:m) {
      if (i != j) {
        Gamma[i, j] <- exp(par[k])
        k <- k + 1
      }
    }
  }
  Gamma <- Gamma / rowSums(Gamma)
  # stationary distribution: solves delta (I - Gamma + 1) = 1
  delta <- solve(t(diag(m) - Gamma + 1), rep(1, m))
  list(lambda = lambda, Gamma = Gamma, delta = delta)
}

hmm_nll <- function(par, x, m) {
  p <- unpack(par, m)
  phi <- p$delta
  ll <- 0
  for (t in 1:length(x)) {
    if (t == 1) {
      v <- phi * dpois(x[t], p$lambda)
    } else {
      v <- (phi %*% p$Gamma) * dpois(x[t], p$lambda)
    }
    u <- sum(v)
    ll <- ll + log(u)
    phi <- v / u
  }
  -ll
}




8.2.4 Question 8: fitting one, two and three states
Question 8 asks for a two-state Poisson HMM fitted to earthquake counts. I fit one, two and three states to the discoveries counts instead, and compare them by AIC and BIC.

fit2 <- optim(c(log(2), log(4), -2, -2), hmm_nll, x = x, m = 2, control = list(maxit = 5000))
fit3 <- optim(c(log(1.5), log(3), log(5), rep(-2, 6)), hmm_nll, x = x, m = 3, control = list(maxit = 10000))

p3 <- unpack(fit3$par, 3)

8.2.6 Forward and backward probabilities
The forward probabilities \(\alpha_t\) and backward probabilities \(\beta_t\) multiply to the same likelihood at every year \(t\). The values here are small (about 3.09e-90), but still well within the range of double precision, so the unscaled version works for 100 observations.
