title: 8  Hidden Markov models
text:
8.3 Reflection
This section I found both fun and very difficult at the same time. The math was very hard to follow and there was a lot of it. The key difference between HMM and SSM is that HMM have discrete state spaces, but the observations can still be continuous or discrete. The idea is similar to SSM, we are trying to use seen observations, which are a random realisation of an underlying process, although in this case that underlying process is a series of discrete states. The goal is to identify which state we are in. The state is hidden and unobserved, we only observe the data.
The coin-toss transition diagram and the transition probability matrix were easy to follow, because they are close to the state space models I had just worked through. The harder part was seeing the joint probability as a product of conditionals, and then how a dependent mixture turns into a likelihood, which I first met with one observation and then with two. The tutorial did not say which exercise to use for the mini-project, so I chose Question 8 and used the discoveries counts, and that choice is why this chapter is built around them.
The hidden states follow a first-order Markov chain, with the transition matrix \(\Gamma\) giving the probability of moving between them and \(\delta\) the starting distribution. Each state has its own Poisson rate, which lets the counts switch between a low and a high level.
The forward algorithm builds the likelihood one year at a time. The values shrink quickly, so I rescale at each step and sum the logs to avoid underflow. I optimise on transformed parameters (\(\log \lambda\) and the logged off-diagonals of \(\Gamma\)) so that the rates stay positive and the rows of \(\Gamma\) still sum to one.
Local decoding picks the most likely state at each year separately. Global decoding, the Viterbi algorithm, finds the most likely whole path. The DAG shows that each state depends only on the one before it, and each count depends only on its own state. An independent mixture draws each year separately, whereas an HMM lets the rate persist from year to year.
The forward and backward probabilities multiply to the same likelihood at every year. To forecast, I take the filtered state probabilities at the end, multiply by \(\Gamma^h\), and mix the two Poissons using those probabilities.
An HMM suits a problem when the counts are overdispersed, the states persist, and the decoded periods make sense. Choosing the number of states comes down to AIC and BIC, and whether the extra state is visited often enough to mean anything. [Add the part you found hardest.] Starting values matter because the likelihood has several local maxima, so I tried more than one.

title: 9  Project 1: Eskom peak demand (SARIMA)
text:
9.1 Summary
Forecasting Eskom peak electricity demand with SARIMA models (Part 1, ARIMA / SARIMA; implementation project; covers real-world data and model comparison).
This project asks which SARIMA model best describes and forecasts the weekly peak of South African electricity demand. I used RSA Contracted Demand (MW) from Eskom’s hourly system data (ESK6816.csv, Eskom Data Portal via Amathuba), 1 April 2019 to September 2023. After removing the missing demand values, I aggregated the hourly data to the daily and then the weekly maximum, because the hourly and daily series were too noisy to show any patterns. I explored the weekly series with seasonal plots, an STL decomposition, lag plots and the ACF and PACF, then identified a SARIMA model by hand and compared it with the model chosen automatically by ARIMA(), using AIC and residual diagnostics, and produced 12-week forecasts.
Weekly peak demand has a clear annual cycle, with a sharp dip in early 2020 during the COVID-19 lockdown. Demand is strongly correlated with Eskom’s own demand forecast (0.966) and negatively correlated with planned outages (−0.637). The ACF decays slowly and rises again towards lag 52, and the PACF cuts off after one spike, which pointed to a SARIMA(1,0,0)(1,0,0)[52]. On a 12-week test set, the automatically selected ARIMA(0,1,2)(1,1,0)[52] forecast best (RMSE 935 MW), while my hand-chosen model (984 MW) did not beat the seasonal naive benchmark (960 MW).
If I did this again, I would add a dummy variable for the lockdown instead of leaving it in the data, and drop the incomplete final week, whose maximum is biased low. Project 3 (Chapter 11) does both for the same data. A full detailed analysis follows below.

title: 9  Project 1: Eskom peak demand (SARIMA)
text:
9.2 Analysis
In this project I will look to determine which SARIMA model provides the best predictions of maximum weekly electricity demand.

9.2.1 EDA
First we will explore the Eskom data, and select only the variables of interest. Our primary variable of concern is \(RSA.Contracted.Demand\), which gives the average electricity demand per hour.
Before exploring the data further, we can see that there are many missing (or na) values in the \(RSA.Contracted.Demand\) variable. This is shown in the plot below, where roughly the last year of demand values are missing.


Code
data <- read.csv("../data/ESK6816.csv")
data <- data |> 
  select(Date.Time.Hour.Beginning, RSA.Contracted.Demand, RSA.Contracted.Forecast, 
         Total.UCLF, Total.OCLF, Total.PCLF, Installed.Eskom.Capacity)
data$DateTime <- ymd_hm(data$Date.Time.Hour.Beginning, tz = "Africa/Johannesburg")

data_tsibble_hourly <- data |> 
  select(-Date.Time.Hour.Beginning) |>   # remove old date / time variable
  relocate(DateTime) |>                  # replace it with properly formatted DateTime
  as_tsibble(index = DateTime)

rm(data) # save pc memory

data_tsibble_hourly |> 
  fill_gaps() |> 
  autoplot(RSA.Contracted.Demand)

Twelve weeks is a short test, so these differences should not be overinterpreted.

title: 9  Project 1: Eskom peak demand (SARIMA)
text:
9.3 Reflection
This was my first substantial project, and I chose the Eskom data because electricity demand affects everyone in South Africa. The hourly data was far too noisy to see any patterns, so I moved to the daily and then the weekly maximum, where the annual cycle became clear. The biggest data problem was the missing demand values in the last year, and the dip during the 2020 lockdown, which I left in the data but which a dummy variable would handle better.
Choosing the SARIMA orders by hand from the ACF and PACF helped me understand what those plots show, but my model forecast worse on the test set than the automatic ARIMA and did not beat seasonal naive, which showed me that a model that looks right from the ACF and PACF does not always forecast best. I came back to the same data in Project 3 (Chapter 11), where I kept the last 12 weeks for testing, added a lockdown dummy and dropped the incomplete final week. That comparison showed me what this first project was missing. I also received feedback on my first draft that I did not have time to fully implement.

title: 10  Project 2: volatility of the rand with GARCH
text:
10.1 Summary
Modelling the volatility of the rand with GARCH models (Part 1, ARCH / GARCH; implementation project; covers real-world data and model comparison).
This project asks whether the USD/ZAR exchange rate shows volatility clustering, which GARCH-type model and error distribution describe it best, and how persistent shocks to the rand’s volatility are. I used daily USD/ZAR closing rates from 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2025, downloaded from Yahoo Finance with quantmod::getSymbols("ZAR=X") and converted to daily log returns in percent, \(r_t = 100 \times \log(P_t / P_{t-1})\), after removing days with missing values and six extreme outlier returns. After exploring the returns and squared returns (ACF, ARCH LM test), I chose a constant mean using the Ljung-Box test and an ARMA comparison. I then fitted GARCH(1,1) models with rugarch using normal, Student t and skewed t errors, added GJR-GARCH and EGARCH, and compared them with QQ plots, AIC/BIC and standardised residual diagnostics.
The returns are uncorrelated but show strong volatility clustering (ARCH LM test \(p < 0.001\)). The best model was a constant mean with GJR-GARCH(1,1) and skewed t errors (\(\hat\xi = 1.18\), \(\hat\nu = 14.7\)), which beat the normal and Student t errors and the symmetric GARCH on AIC and BIC. Volatility rises mostly after positive returns (rand weakening), since \(\hat\delta = -0.037\) almost cancels \(\hat\alpha_1 = 0.042\) for negative shocks, and persistence is very high (\(\hat\rho = 0.9956\), half-life about 158 days). The predicted price is essentially the previous day’s price, so the model’s value is the changing width of the prediction band rather than the point forecast.
If I did this again, I would address three limitations. The residual tests still show weak short-lag dependence in the squared residuals, and GJR(2,1) and (1,2) did not remove it, so I would try other variance structures. The long-run volatility is poorly estimated (0.72% against a sample standard deviation of 0.96%), because persistence is near one and \(\hat\alpha_0\) is not significant. I would also refit before and after 2020 to check for a structural break, and evaluate the forecasts out of sample. A full detailed analysis follows below.

title: 10  Project 2: volatility of the rand with GARCH
text:
10.2 Data and EDA

10.2.1 Downloading the data
This project used ARCH and GARCH models to analyse the volatility of daily USD/ZAR exchange rate data from 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2025. The data was downloaded from Yahoo Finance using the quantmod package, and days with missing values were removed from the data set. Each observation is the daily closing USD/ZAR exchange rate (rand per US dollar), which is the rate at the end of that day’s trading.


Code
library(quantmod)
library(rugarch)
library(FinTS)
library(here)
library(tidyverse)

file_path <- here("data", "usdzar.csv")

if (!file.exists(file_path)) {
  zar <- getSymbols("ZAR=X", src = "yahoo", from = "2015-01-01", to = "2025-12-31",
                    auto.assign = FALSE)
  zar <- Cl(zar)
  write.csv(data.frame(date = index(zar), exchange_rate = as.numeric(zar)), file_path, row.names = FALSE)
}

data <- read.csv(file_path)
sapply(data, class)
data$date <- as.Date(data$date)
nrow(data)
range(data$date)
sum(is.na(data))
data <- na.omit(data)
nrow(data)
range(data$date)
sum(is.na(data))




10.2.2 EDA and outliers
Our first step is to analyse the data visually. Figure 10.1 below plots the exchange rate (or the price level) at close for each day over the time period of interest.


Code
plot(data$date, data$exchange_rate, type = "l", xlab = "time", ylab = "rands per dollar (price level)")








Figure 10.1: Daily USD/ZAR exchange rates





The upward trend over time in Figure 10.1 above shows that over the 11 years from the start of 2015 to the end of 2025, the exchange rate increased. One dollar only was worth roughly R12, but at the end one dollar was worth nearly R18. The value of the Rand has an inverse relationship with the USD/ZAR exchange rate, and thus the value of the Rand relative to the dollar decreased over this period as the price level increased. As there is a clear trend, the data is not stationary. We can confirm this with a Ljung-Box test for autocorrelation.


Code
Box.test(data$exchange_rate, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")



    Box-Ljung test

data:  data$exchange_rate
X-squared = 27705, df = 10, p-value < 2.2e-16


The p-value < 0.001 shows there is significant evidence of autocorrelation.
When working with financial data, we are usually more interested in returns \(r_t\) than price levels \(P_t\). There are three types of returns. Simple return shows the percentage change in the price. Gross returns are ratio amount by which the price level increased or decreased from one day to the next. Logarithmic returns show the log of the gross returns and are most preferable as you can add log returns over time to get the total return for that period. Figure 10.2 below shows simple and log returns for our data.


Code
data$simple_return      <- c(NA, 100 * diff(data$exchange_rate) / head(data$exchange_rate, -1))
data$gross_return       <- 1 + data$simple_return / 100
data$logarithmic_return <- 100 * log(data$gross_return)
returns <- data$logarithmic_return[-1] # first value is always NA

par(mfrow = c(2, 1))
plot(data$date, data$simple_return, type = "l", xlab = "", ylab = "R_t",
     main = "Simple returns")
plot(data$date, data$logarithmic_return, type = "l", xlab = "", ylab = "r_t",
     main = "Logarithmic returns")








Figure 10.2: Daily simple returns in percent (top) and logarithmic returns in percent (bottom), before cleaning.





In Figure 10.2 above, we see that differencing has removed the upward trend that was present on the price level data. However, there are several returns around November 2024 and January 2025 that are drastically different from the others. If we look at how the return data is distributed, we see that the data looks normally distributed around 0, with some outliers reaching positive and minus 20. This is evident in Figure 10.3 below.

Because the price reverts straight back, these look like data errors rather than genuine movements in the rand, so we remove them.
After identifying the outliers, we remove them from the data, and repeat our plots of the data as we did previously to see how things now look. Each of these plots are shown in Figure 10.6 below.

  filter(abs(logarithmic_return) <= 5)

We can clearly see from each of the plots in Figure 10.6 above that there are no further clear outliers, and we are ready to begin our analysis.


10.2.3 ACF of returns and squared returns
Next, we check for evidence of volatility clustering in the logarithmic return data (from now on referred to as “returns”). We do this by using ACF plots of the returns, as shown in Figure 10.7 below.


Code
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
acf(returns, main = "returns")
acf(returns^2, main = "squared returns")








Figure 10.7: ACF plot of logarithmic returns (left) and squared logarithmic returns (right)





In addition to the above Figure 10.7, we also perform an ARCH LM test to check if the squared residuals have significant autocorrelation.


Code
ArchTest(returns, lags = 12)



    ARCH LM-test; Null hypothesis: no ARCH effects

data:  returns
Chi-squared = 118.1, df = 12, p-value < 2.2e-16


The ARCH test checks for conditional heteroscedasticity in the data. The ACF returns plot shows there is little or no significant correlation at any lags. The couple significant spikes are expected due to random chance when checking over 30 lags. However, the ACF on the squared residuals shows that there are many significant lags. In addition, the ARCH LM test show that there is significant autocorrelation among squared residuals within the first 12 lags. These findings are both evidence that there is volatility clustering in the data, and that the magnitude of a shock is not independent of the magnitude of previous shocks.

title: 10  Project 2: volatility of the rand with GARCH
text:
10.3 ARCH / GARCH Models
ARCH / GARCH models have two components, where the returns \(r_t\) are a combination of a mean equation \(\mu_t\) and a variance equation \(\varepsilon_t\), which gives us,
\[r_t = \mu_t + \varepsilon_t.\]
The aim of our model is to choose mean and variance equations that best explain our data \(r_t\).

10.3.1 Mean Equation
First we have our mean equation \(\mu_t\). We have two options for our mean equation, either we can use a constant mean,
\[\mu_t = \mu,\]
or we can model the mean using an ARMA(p, q) model,
\[\mu_t = \mu + \sum_{i=1}^{p} \phi_i r_{t-i} + \sum_{j=1}^{q} \theta_j \varepsilon_{t-j}\]
We use a Ljung-Box test to check for autocorrelation in the log returns.


Code
Box.test(returns, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")



    Box-Ljung test

data:  returns
X-squared = 9.7938, df = 10, p-value = 0.4588


The Ljung-Box test has a p-value of 0.4588. There is not enough evidence to suggest that there is autocorrelation in the data, even at a 0.1 significance level. Thus, a constant mean is adequate for the returns.
We can investigate further by fitting multiple ARMA models to the data to confirm if a constant mean, an ARMA(0,0), is the best choice. We compare ARMA(0,0), ARMA(1,0), ARMA(0,1), and ARMA(1,1) in Table 10.2 below.


Code
ARMA_00 <- arima(returns, order = c(0,0,0), include.mean = TRUE)
ARMA_10 <- arima(returns, order = c(1,0,0), include.mean = TRUE)
ARMA_01 <- arima(returns, order = c(0,0,1), include.mean = TRUE)
ARMA_11 <- arima(returns, order = c(1,0,1), include.mean = TRUE)

data.frame(
  Model      = c("ARMA(0,0)", "ARMA(1,0)", "ARMA(0,1)", "ARMA(1,1)"),
  Parameters = c(2, 3, 3, 4),
  LogLik     = round(c(logLik(ARMA_00), logLik(ARMA_10), logLik(ARMA_01), logLik(ARMA_11)), 2),
  AIC        = round(c(AIC(ARMA_00), AIC(ARMA_10), AIC(ARMA_01), AIC(ARMA_11)), 2),
  BIC        = round(c(BIC(ARMA_00), BIC(ARMA_10), BIC(ARMA_01), BIC(ARMA_11)), 2))




Table 10.2: Log-likelihood, AIC and BIC for four ARMA models for the mean of the returns.

From Table 10.2 above we see that there is little difference in log-likelihood between the models, and that the gains from adding more model parameters is minimal. In addition, both AIC and BIC scores increase as model complexity increases, indicating the increase performance is due to fitting the noise in the data. Based on this comparison, best form for the mean equation is a constant mean.
However, the ARIMA model assumes constant variance, which is not an assumption made in GARCH models. The coefficient for \(\mu\) from the ARMA(0,0) will not equal the \(\mu\) found by a GARCH model that assumes a constant mean. As our ARMA models suggest a constant mean, and our Ljung-Box test showed there was no significant autocorrelation in the data, for our model, we will use a constant mean in our mean equation. This gives us the following,
\[\mu_t = \mu, \qquad \text{and}\]
\[r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t.\]


10.3.2 Variance Equation
Next we have our variance (or shock) equation,
\[\varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} (0, 1)\]
In the above variance equation, we have \(z_t\) the random white noise error term, and we have our conditional variance term \(\sigma_t\) which we derive as follows,
\[\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{q} \alpha_i \varepsilon_{t-i}^2 + \sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j \sigma_{t-j}^2.\]
Like the mean equation, we want to choose a variance equation that describes how the conditional variance of \(r_t\) changes over time, so that the uncertainty around our predictions of \(r_t\) is more realistic. If the variance was not conditional over time, we would have,
\[
\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 = 1, \qquad \text{making} \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t =z_t.
\]
As our above ARCH LM-test and ACF plot of squared residuals both suggest there is conditional variance, we will use a GARCH model. In most cases, a GARCH(1,1) is most suitable, so we will start with that form in our modeling. This, in addition to our constant mean model, gives us the following for \(r_t = \mu_t + \varepsilon_t\),
\[\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2\]
\[\therefore \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t = \sqrt{\alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2}\; z_t\]
\[\therefore \qquad  r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t = \mu + \sqrt{\alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2}\; z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} D(0, 1).\]
In addition to estimating parameters for the variance equation \(\alpha_0\), \(\alpha_1\) and \(\beta_1\), we also have to choose a distribution \(D\) for the error term \(z_t\), which can be modelled using either a normal distribution, or a student-t distribution. Determining which form of variance equation to use will be done during modeling below.

title: 10  Project 2: volatility of the rand with GARCH
text:
10.4 rugarch Models
Having chosen a constant mean, we use the rugarch package to fit a GARCH(1,1) variance equation. We use GARCH(1,1) as it is the standard specification and higher orders add extra parameters without improving model performance. The general GARCH(p, q) model with a constant mean has the parameters,
\[\theta = (\mu,\ \alpha_0,\ \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_q,\ \beta_1, \dots, \beta_p),\]
which for GARCH(1,1) gives us,
\[r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} D(0,1),\]
\[\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2,\]
\[\theta = (\mu,\ \alpha_0,\ \alpha_1,\ \beta_1).\]
We estimate the \(\theta\) parameters using maximum likelihood.

10.4.1 Normally Distributed Errors
We first fit the model with normal errors, \(z_t \sim N(0, 1)\), and use a quantile plot of the standardised residuals to check whether a heavier-tailed distribution is needed. This is shown in Figure 10.8 below.


Code
make_spec <- function(model, dist) {
  ugarchspec(variance.model = list(model = model, garchOrder = c(1, 1)),
             mean.model = list(armaOrder = c(0, 0), include.mean = TRUE),
             distribution.model = dist)
}

fit_n <- ugarchfit(make_spec("sGARCH", "norm"), data = returns)
round(fit_n@fit$robust.matcoef, 4)


        Estimate  Std. Error  t value Pr(>|t|)
mu        0.0067      0.0155   0.4300   0.6672
omega     0.0074      0.0038   1.9507   0.0511
alpha1    0.0366      0.0045   8.2079   0.0000
beta1     0.9555      0.0021 465.1679   0.0000


Code
z_n <- as.numeric(residuals(fit_n, standardize = TRUE))

qqnorm(z_n, main = "QQ plot of standardised residuals (normal GARCH)")
qqline(z_n, col = "red")








Figure 10.8: QQ plot of the standardised residuals of the GARCH(1,1) model with normal errors.





The QQ plot in Figure 10.8 shows that most of the standardised residuals follow what we would expect under normality, but the right tail is heavier than the normal distribution would predict.


10.4.2 Student-t Errors
We therefore refit with Student t errors, which adds the degrees of freedom \(\nu\) (smaller \(\nu\) means heavier tails), giving us the follow,
\[r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} t_\nu,\]
\[\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2,\]
\[\theta = (\mu,\ \alpha_0,\ \alpha_1,\ \beta_1,\ \nu).\]
The QQ plot using Student t distributed residuals is shown in Figure 10.9 below.


Code
fit_t <- ugarchfit(make_spec("sGARCH", "std"), data = returns)
round(fit_t@fit$robust.matcoef, 4)


        Estimate  Std. Error  t value Pr(>|t|)
mu       -0.0058      0.0154  -0.3791   0.7046
omega     0.0060      0.0035   1.7010   0.0889
alpha1    0.0389      0.0043   9.0732   0.0000
beta1     0.9549      0.0019 506.3316   0.0000
shape    12.6360      2.5972   4.8652   0.0000


Code
# QQ plot of the standardised residuals against the fitted t distribution
z_t <- as.numeric(residuals(fit_t, standardize = TRUE))
nu  <- coef(fit_t)["shape"]
n   <- length(z_t)

qqplot(qt(ppoints(n), nu) * sqrt((nu - 2) / nu), z_t,
       xlab = "Theoretical t quantiles", ylab = "Standardised residuals",
       main = "QQ plot against fitted t (GARCH-t)")
abline(0, 1, col = "red")








Figure 10.9: QQ plot of the standardised residuals against the fitted Student t distribution.





In Figure 10.9 above, the QQ plot of the Student t model shows an improvement, as the right tail is now closer to the red line. However, the left tail is now lighter than the fitted t expects, while the right tail is still slightly heavier. This suggests that the tails are asymmetric.


10.4.3 Skew Student-t Errors
The Student t is symmetric, so it cannot fit both tails at once. To address this, we will fit a model using a skew Student-t distribution, which adds a skewness parameter \(\xi\), which gives the following,
\[r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{skew-}t_{\xi,\nu},\]
\[\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2,\]
\[\theta = (\mu,\ \alpha_0,\ \alpha_1,\ \beta_1,\ \xi,\ \nu).\]
We again use a QQ plot to assess the model fit, as shown in Figure 10.10 below.


Code
fit_st <- ugarchfit(make_spec("sGARCH", "sstd"), data = returns)
round(fit_st@fit$robust.matcoef, 4)


        Estimate  Std. Error  t value Pr(>|t|)
mu        0.0081      0.0157   0.5139   0.6073
omega     0.0042      0.0030   1.4255   0.1540
alpha1    0.0371      0.0036  10.1772   0.0000
beta1     0.9587      0.0010 914.5102   0.0000
skew      1.1696      0.0339  34.4991   0.0000
shape    13.8018      2.9456   4.6856   0.0000


Code
# QQ plot of the standardised residuals against the fitted skewed t distribution
z_st <- as.numeric(residuals(fit_st, standardize = TRUE))
q_st <- qdist("sstd", p = ppoints(length(z_st)), mu = 0, sigma = 1,
              skew = coef(fit_st)["skew"], shape = coef(fit_st)["shape"])

qqplot(q_st, z_st,
       xlab = "Theoretical skewed t quantiles", ylab = "Standardised residuals",
       main = "QQ plot against fitted skewed t (GARCH-skewed t)")
abline(0, 1, col = "red")








Figure 10.10: QQ plot of the standardised residuals against the fitted skewed t distribution.







10.4.4 Model Comparison
The three models share the same mean and variance equations, they only differ in the distribution of \(z_t\). The normal has no extra parameters, the Student t adds \(\nu\), and the skewed t adds \(\xi\) as well. We compare the AIC and BIC scores of the three models in Table 10.3 below.


Code
ic <- cbind( # comparing the normal, t and skewed t fits
  GARCH_normal = infocriteria(fit_n)[1:2, 1],
  GARCH_t      = infocriteria(fit_t)[1:2, 1],
  GARCH_sstd   = infocriteria(fit_st)[1:2, 1]
)
round(ic, 4) |> as.data.frame()




Table 10.3: AIC and BIC (per observation) for the three error distributions.








GARCH_normal
GARCH_t
GARCH_sstd

For both AIC and BIC in Table 10.3 above, the GARCH model using skew Student t errors outperforms the models with normal errors and the student t errors. Given the QQ plot on the skew Student t model was also the best, we will use skew Student t errors in our model, which gives us the following final model,
\[r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \text{with errors},\]
\[\varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{skew-}t_{\xi,\nu} \text{ (0, 1)}, \qquad \text{where},\]
\[\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2, \qquad \text{and parameters},\]
\[\theta = (\mu,\ \alpha_0,\ \alpha_1,\ \beta_1,\ \xi,\ \nu).\]


10.4.5 GJR-GARCH and EGARCH
The GARCH(1,1) variance equation depends on \(\varepsilon_{t-1}^2\), so it responds identically to positive and negative shocks of the same size (§7.11). The skewed t errors allow the two tails of \(z_t\) to differ, but they do not change this. To allow the variance to respond asymmetrically (the leverage effect), we fit two asymmetric GARCH models, GJR-GARCH and EGARCH, keeping skewed t errors. Both have the same mean equation and error distribution,
\[r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{skew-}t_{\xi,\nu},\]
and differ in the variance equation. The GJR-GARCH adds a term that is switched on only for negative shocks,
\[\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \left(\alpha_1 + \delta\,\mathbb{1}[\varepsilon_{t-1}<0]\right)\varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2,\]
\[\theta = (\mu,\ \alpha_0,\ \alpha_1,\ \beta_1,\ \delta,\ \xi,\ \nu),\]
while the EGARCH models the log of the variance, so no positivity restrictions are needed,
\[\ln \sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \beta_1 \ln \sigma_{t-1}^2 + \alpha_1\left(|z_{t-1}| - E|z_{t-1}|\right) + \delta z_{t-1},\]
\[\theta = (\mu,\ \alpha_0,\ \alpha_1,\ \beta_1,\ \delta,\ \xi,\ \nu).\]
In both models \(\delta\) is the asymmetry parameter, and we keep an asymmetric model only if \(\hat\delta\) is significant and the information criteria agree. Note that rugarch labels the EGARCH terms differently, its alpha1 is \(\delta\) (sign) and its gamma1 is \(\alpha_1\) (size). We again use QQ plots to assess the fit of both models, as shown in Figure 10.11 below.


Code
fit_gjr    <- ugarchfit(make_spec("gjrGARCH", "sstd"), data = returns)
fit_egarch <- ugarchfit(make_spec("eGARCH",   "sstd"), data = returns)

Table 10.4 shows that both GJR and EGARCH outperform our GARCH model. EGARCH fits marginally better than GJR, but the difference in log-likelihood (0.72) is negligible. As GJR is easier to interpret than EGARCH, and it outperforms our GARCH model, we will use the GJR model. Our model is now as follows,
\[r_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{skew-}t_{\xi,\nu}\ (0,1),\]
\[\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \left(\alpha_1 + \delta\,\mathbb{1}[\varepsilon_{t-1}<0]\right)\varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1\sigma_{t-1}^2,\]

By subbing in our estimates from Table 10.5 above into our model, we get,
\[\hat\theta = (\hat\mu = 0.0186,\ \hat\alpha_0 = 0.0023,\ \hat\alpha_1 = 0.0421,\ \hat\beta_1 = 0.9731,\ \hat\delta = -0.0374,\ \hat\xi = 1.1786,\ \hat\nu = 14.6627),\]
\[\therefore\ r_t = 0.0186 + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{skew-}t_{\xi=1.1786,\ \nu=14.6627}\ (0,1),\]
\[\therefore\ \sigma_t^2 = 0.0023 + \left(0.0421 - 0.0374\,\mathbb{1}[\varepsilon_{t-1}<0]\right)\varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + 0.9731\,\sigma_{t-1}^2.\]
The errors (or innovations) are modelled as skewed Student t with \(\hat\xi = 1.18\) and \(\hat\nu = 14.7\). Since \(\hat\xi > 1\), large positive standardised shocks (rand depreciation) are more frequent than large negative ones, and \(\hat\nu = 14.7\) indicates tails that are heavier than a normal distribution. To check whether the skew is significant, we test \(\xi = 1\) (a symmetric distribution) using \(t = (\hat\xi - 1)/SE\).

10.6 Residual Diagnostics
Now that we have our model, we check the standardised residuals and the squared standardised residuals for any remaining dependence or ARCH effects. Figure 10.12 shows the residuals and their ACFs, and Table 10.7 shows the tests below.


Code
z <- as.numeric(residuals(fit_final, standardize = TRUE))

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(z, pch = 16, cex = 0.3, xlab = "Time", ylab = "Standardised residual",
     main = "Standardised residuals")
acf(z,      main = "ACF of standardised residuals")
acf(z^2,    main = "ACF of squared standardised residuals")
acf(abs(z), main = "ACF of absolute standardised residuals")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))








Figure 10.12: Standardised residuals of the GJR-GARCH model over time, and the ACFs of the standardised, squared and absolute standardised residuals.







Code
diag_tab <- data.frame(
  Test = c("Ljung-Box on z (mean equation)",
           "Ljung-Box on z^2 (variance equation)",
           "Ljung-Box on |z|",
           "ARCH LM test on z"),
  p_value = c(Box.test(z,      lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value,
              Box.test(z^2,    lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value,
              Box.test(abs(z), lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value,
              ArchTest(z, lags = 10)$p.value)
)
transform(diag_tab, p_value = round(p_value, 3))

In Figure 10.12, the standardised residuals plot shows no obvious pattern or volatility clustering. The ACF of standardised residuals has only a few isolated lags just outside the bounds, and the Ljung-Box test finds no overall autocorrelation, so there is no evidence of any remaining linear dependence. The ACFs of squared and absolute standardised residuals show significant lags at the first few lags (lags 1 and 2 for both, plus lag 3 for the absolute residuals and lag 10 for the squared residuals), so there may be some remaining weak short-lag dependence in volatility. Table 10.7 shows that the mean equation is adequate (Ljung-Box on \(\hat z_t\), \(p = 0.65\)), but the Ljung-Box tests on \(\hat z_t^2\) and \(|\hat z_t|\) and the ARCH LM test are significant (\(p \le 0.009\)). Together with the ACFs, this indicates weak, short-lag volatility dependence that the GJR-GARCH(1,1) does not capture, which we will treat as a limitation.

title: 10  Project 2: volatility of the rand with GARCH
text:
10.7 Persistence
We are interested in how long the effect of a shock persists. For the standard GARCH(1,1) model, \(\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1\varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1\sigma_{t-1}^2\), the persistence is how slowly a volatility shock fades (close to 1 means very slowly), and is defined as,
\[\rho = \alpha_1 + \beta_1.\]
If \(\rho < 1\), the unconditional variance is the long-run average variance that volatility reverts to, and is calculated as,
\[\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_t) = E(\sigma_t^2) = \frac{\alpha_0}{1-\rho}.\]
The long-run daily volatility is the square root of the unconditional variance, and is the typical size of a daily move in percent. The half-life of a volatility shock is the number of days for its effect to halve, and is approximately,
\[h_{1/2} = \frac{\log(0.5)}{\log(\rho)}, \qquad 0 < \rho < 1.\]
Our model differs in its variance equation, which has the extra asymmetry term,
\[\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \left(\alpha_1 + \delta\,\mathbb{1}[\varepsilon_{t-1}<0]\right)\varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1\sigma_{t-1}^2.\]
Negative shocks carry the extra effect \(\delta\), so they enter the persistence as well. With about half of the shocks negative, the persistence becomes
\[\rho = \alpha_1 + \frac{\delta}{2} + \beta_1.\]
We use the same expressions for the unconditional variance and half-life with this \(\rho\).


Code
data.frame(
  Measure = c("Persistence", "Half-life (trading days)", "Long-run variance", "Long-run volatility (% per day)"),
  Value   = round(c(persistence(fit_final),
                    log(0.5) / log(persistence(fit_final)),
                    uncvariance(fit_final),
                    sqrt(uncvariance(fit_final))), 4)
)




Table 10.8: Persistence, half-life, long-run variance and long-run volatility of the final model.







Measure
Value




Persistence

157.8200


Long-run variance
0.5181


Long-run volatility (% per day)
0.7198









We take the estimates in Table 10.8 from rugarch, which computes the share of negative shocks from the fitted skewed t distribution, giving \(\hat\rho = 0.9956\), a long-run variance of \(0.518\) (a volatility of \(0.72\%\) per day) and a half-life of about \(158\) trading days. Persistence this close to 1 means shocks to volatility fade very slowly, with the effect of a shock taking about seven to eight months to halve, so periods of high or low volatility last a long time. The estimated reaction to a positive shock is \(\hat\alpha_1 = 0.042\) and the memory of past volatility is \(\hat\beta_1 = 0.973\), while \(\hat\delta = -0.037\) (significant) cuts the effect of a negative shock to \(\hat\alpha_1 + \hat\delta = 0.005\), so volatility rises mostly after positive returns, when the rand weakens.
The mean \(\hat\mu = 0.0186\) is the average daily return, about 0.02% a day. This is tiny compared with the typical daily move of 0.7% to 1%, so the rand barely drifts on average and the day-to-day changes are mostly noise, as for a random walk. The constant \(\hat\alpha_0 = 0.0023\) is the fixed amount added to the variance each day, regardless of the previous shock. It is small on its own, but the long-run variance divides it by \(1 - \rho = 0.0044\), which gives \(0.0023 / 0.0044 \approx 0.52\). This also explains why the long-run level is so uncertain, as when \(\rho\) is close to 1, a small change in the estimates makes a large change in that division.

text:
10.8 Volatility Forecast
Having fitted the model, we look at its estimated conditional volatility over time and at its 20-day volatility forecast, shown in Figure 10.13 below.


Code
rdates <- data_clean$date[-1]      # dates that match `returns`
long_run <- sqrt(uncvariance(fit_final))

fc <- ugarchforecast(fit_final, n.ahead = 20)
sig_f <- as.numeric(sigma(fc))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

plot(rdates, as.numeric(sigma(fit_final)), type = "l", xlab = "",
     ylab = "conditional sd (%)", main = "Estimated daily volatility")
abline(h = long_run, col = "red", lty = 2)

plot(1:20, sig_f, type = "b", pch = 16, xlab = "days ahead",
     ylab = "forecast volatility (% per day)", main = "20-day forecast",
     ylim = range(sig_f, long_run))
abline(h = long_run, col = "red", lty = 2)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))








Figure 10.13: Estimated daily conditional volatility of USD/ZAR (left) and the 20-day volatility forecast (right) from the GJR-GARCH(1,1) model with skewed t errors. The dashed line is the long-run volatility.





The left panel of Figure 10.13 shows that the estimated volatility of the rand moves in clear waves. It peaks in 2016 and 2018, at about 1.5% a day, and most sharply in early 2020 at about 1.75% (this is possibly related to COVID-19 which started in 2020), and then falls back each time. Volatility is above the model’s long-run level of 0.72% for most of the sample, and falls to its lowest point, about 0.5% a day, by the end of 2025.
Because volatility is currently low, the 20-day forecast in the right panel rises from 0.48% to 0.50% a day, heading towards the long-run level. It rises only slowly, since persistence is close to 1, so only a small part of the gap closes in 20 days. The forecast says nothing about the direction of the rand, only about how large daily moves are likely to be.


Code
data.frame(
  Measure = c("Sample standard deviation of returns",
              "Average fitted volatility",
              "Model's long-run volatility"),
  Value   = round(c(sd(returns),
                    mean(as.numeric(sigma(fit_final))),
                    sqrt(uncvariance(fit_final))), 2)
)




Table 10.9: Sample standard deviation of the returns, average fitted volatility and the model’s long-run volatility (% per day).







Measure
Value




Sample standard deviation of returns
0.96


Average fitted volatility
0.94


Model’s long-run volatility
0.72









Table 10.9 shows that the model’s implied long-run volatility is 0.72% per day, but the sample standard deviation of the returns is 0.96% and the average fitted volatility is 0.94%, so the model’s long-run level is probably underestimated, because it depends on \(\hat\alpha_0\) (not significant) and on persistence very close to one.

title: 10  Project 2: volatility of the rand with GARCH
section: 10.9 Model Predictions and Actual Data Comparison
text:
10.9 Model Predictions and Actual Data Comparison
We now compare our model, including the conditional variance for our prediction intervals, with our actual data, shown in Figure 10.14 below.


Code
mu_hat <- coef(fit_final)["mu"]
s      <- as.numeric(sigma(fit_final))
p_prev <- data_clean$exchange_rate[-nrow(data_clean)]
p_act  <- data_clean$exchange_rate[-1]

band <- tibble(date = rdates, price = p_act, r = returns,
               pred = p_prev * exp(mu_hat / 100),
               lo   = p_prev * exp((mu_hat - 2 * s) / 100),
               hi   = p_prev * exp((mu_hat + 2 * s) / 100),
               r_lo = mu_hat - 2 * s, r_hi = mu_hat + 2 * s)

band_both <- bind_rows(
  band |> mutate(panel = "Full sample"),
  band |> filter(date >= as.Date("2025-01-01")) |> mutate(panel = "Most recent year (2025)")
) |>
  mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = c("Full sample", "Most recent year (2025)")),
         pred  = ifelse(panel == "Full sample", NA_real_, pred))

ggplot(band_both, aes(date)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi, fill = "95% prediction band"), alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = pred, colour = "Predicted price"), linetype = "dashed",
            linewidth = 0.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = price, colour = "Actual price"), linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("95% prediction band" = "red")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Actual price" = "black", "Predicted price" = "blue")) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "", y = "rand per dollar", fill = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 10.14: Actual USD/ZAR price, one-day-ahead predicted price and the 95% prediction band from the GJR-GARCH model: full sample (top) and the most recent year (bottom).





The predicted price is essentially yesterday’s price, as expected for an exchange rate whose returns are uncorrelated, so the model’s contribution is the width of the prediction band. Over the full sample the band is widest around early 2020, and in 2025 it widens in April and then narrows steadily as the year becomes calmer.
crumbs: 10  Project 2: volatility of the rand with GARCH

title: 10  Project 2: volatility of the rand with GARCH
text:
10.10 Fitted Volatility
Figure 10.15 plots the daily returns against plus and minus two fitted conditional standard deviations from our model (red), and against the band that a constant-variance model would give (blue, plus and minus two sample standard deviations).


Code
m        <- mean(returns)
sd_const <- sd(returns)

ggplot(band_both, aes(date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = r, colour = "Daily return"), linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = m + 2 * sd_const, colour = "Constant-variance band"), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = m - 2 * sd_const, colour = "Constant-variance band"), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = r_hi, colour = "GJR-GARCH band"), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = r_lo, colour = "GJR-GARCH band"), linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Daily return" = "grey50",
                                 "GJR-GARCH band" = "red",
                                 "Constant-variance band" = "blue")) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "", y = "daily log return (%)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 10.15: Daily log returns with the 95% prediction band from the GJR-GARCH model and the constant-variance band: full sample (top) and the most recent year 2025 (bottom).





The constant-variance band is the same width throughout, so it is too narrow in turbulent periods (such as 2016 and early 2020, when many returns fall outside it) and too wide in calm ones, whereas the GARCH band widens and narrows with the volatility, reaching about ±3.5% in early 2020 and narrowing to about ±1% by the end of the sample.
crumbs: 10  Project 2: volatility of the rand with GARCH

title: 10  Project 2: volatility of the rand with GARCH
text:
10.11 Price Forecast
Finally, we use the model to forecast the exchange rate 20 trading days beyond the end of the data. Figure 10.16 shows the last three months of 2025 and the forecast price with its 95% prediction band. As the daily returns are uncorrelated, the variances add up over the horizon, so the band at day \(h\) uses the cumulative variance \(\sum_{k=1}^{h} \hat\sigma_{T+k}^2\).


Code
p_last <- tail(data_clean$exchange_rate, 1)
d_last <- tail(data_clean$date, 1)
h      <- 1:20
cum_sd <- sqrt(cumsum(sig_f^2))   # sd of the cumulative return over h days

fdates <- seq(d_last + 1, by = "day", length.out = 40)
fdates <- fdates[as.integer(format(fdates, "%u")) <= 5][1:20]   # weekdays only

fc_tab <- tibble(date = fdates,
                 pred = p_last * exp(mu_hat * h / 100),
                 lo   = p_last * exp((mu_hat * h - 2 * cum_sd) / 100),
                 hi   = p_last * exp((mu_hat * h + 2 * cum_sd) / 100))

recent <- band |> filter(date >= as.Date("2025-10-01"))

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = recent, aes(date, price, colour = "Actual price")) +
  geom_ribbon(data = fc_tab, aes(date, ymin = lo, ymax = hi, fill = "95% prediction band"), alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(data = fc_tab, aes(date, pred, colour = "Forecast price"), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("95% prediction band" = "red")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Actual price" = "black", "Forecast price" = "blue")) +
  labs(x = "", y = "rand per dollar", fill = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 10.16: Actual USD/ZAR price for the last three months of 2025, and the 20-day-ahead price forecast with its 95% prediction band from the GJR-GARCH model.





The forecast price is almost flat at about R16.6 per dollar, which is essentially the last observed price. It rises very slightly because the estimated mean return is a small positive drift (\(\hat\mu = 0.0186\%\) a day), which adds up to only about 0.4% over 20 days, much smaller than the width of the band. The model’s information is in the band, which starts at about R16.4 to R16.7 on day 1 and widens to about R15.9 to R17.4 by day 20. It widens because uncertainty accumulates over the days, which makes the band a cone rather than parallel lines. The forecast says nothing about the direction of the rand, only how far it could plausibly move.
The volatility forecast and prediction bands are useful for risk management, for example setting risk limits and value-at-risk figures that tighten in calm periods and widen in turbulent ones, or deciding how much exposure to the rand to hedge. They have limits, though. They say nothing about the direction of the rand, since the point forecast is essentially the last price. The residual tests showed some remaining volatility dependence the model misses. The long-run level is poorly estimated, and the forecasts rely on the 2015 to 2025 data, so they cannot anticipate a sudden event or structural break such as the April 2025 spike.
crumbs: 10  Project 2: volatility of the rand with GARCH

title: 10  Project 2: volatility of the rand with GARCH
text:
10.12 Reflection
The hardest part was keeping apart ideas that sound similar. I first thought that skewed t errors and the GJR-GARCH or EGARCH models did the same job, since both are about asymmetry, but they are not the same thing. The skewed t describes the shape of the error distribution \(z_t\) (whether large positive and negative standardised shocks are equally likely), while GJR and EGARCH change how the variance reacts to the sign of the previous shock. Once I separated them I could fit and compare both properly. I also found that packages and textbooks use different parameterisations. In rugarch, the EGARCH alpha1 is the sign term and gamma1 the size term, which is the reverse of my notes, so I had to check the formulas against the output rather than trust the names.
Residual diagnostics took me a long time. I did not expect the model to still show dependence after a good QQ plot and good information criteria. I had to work out that the Ljung-Box test on \(\hat z_t\) checks the mean equation and the test on \(\hat z_t^2\) checks the variance equation, which showed my mean equation was fine while a little volatility dependence remained. I tried GJR(2,1) and GJR(1,2) to remove it, and neither did, so I report it as a limitation rather than hide it. I also had to learn that persistence for the GJR model is not simply \(\alpha_1 + \beta_1\), and that the long-run variance can be badly estimated when persistence is close to one, as my 0.72% a day is well below the sample standard deviation of 0.96%.
Through this project I learned that choosing a model is a sequence of small decisions, each backed by evidence. For example, a constant mean from the Ljung-Box test and ARMA comparison, skewed t errors from QQ plots and AIC/BIC, and GJR over EGARCH because the fit was almost the same and GJR is easier to interpret. I also learned how to read the output, such as testing the skew with \((\hat\xi - 1)/SE\) rather than the package’s p-value, which tests against zero. Plotting the model against the data taught me the most about what GARCH does. The point forecast of an exchange rate is just yesterday’s price, and the value of the model is in the width of the band, which was widest in early 2020 and in the April 2025 spike. A constant-variance band has the same overall coverage, but it misses far more of the turbulent days.
If I did this again, I would first try other variance structures to deal with the leftover dependence. I would refit the model before and after 2020 to check for a structural break, and evaluate the forecasts out of sample instead of only fitting in sample. I planned to write my own GARCH(1,1) log-likelihood and compare it to rugarch, but dropped it because of time, so my estimates rely on the package. I would also use a news impact curve to show the asymmetry visually, and I would investigate the six extreme returns I removed, to see whether they are data errors or real market events, rather than simply excluding them.
The most interesting result for me was that a model with an almost-zero mean and strongly persistent volatility describes the rand well, which matches what I’d expect of an exchange rate that moves like a random walk with changing risk.
crumbs: 10  Project 2: volatility of the rand with GARCH

title: 11  Project 3: Explaining and forecasting Eskom weekly peak demand with time series regression
text:
11.1 Summary
Explaining and forecasting weekly peak electricity demand with time series regression (Part 2, time series regression; implementation project; covers real-world data, model comparison and computational / statistical programming).
This project asks which factors explain the weekly peak of South African electricity demand, and whether allowing for autocorrelated errors changes which factors matter, how precisely they are estimated, and how well the model forecasts. We used the weekly maximum of RSA Contracted Demand (MW) from Eskom’s hourly system data, 1 April 2019 to 4 September 2023 (232 complete weeks), together with Eskom’s planned, unplanned and other outages, a public-holiday calendar, a lockdown dummy and weekly temperatures for Johannesburg, Pretoria and Durban from the Open-Meteo archive. All modelling choices were made on the first 220 weeks, and the last 12 weeks were kept for testing.
The residuals of the ordinary regression are strongly autocorrelated (Ljung–Box \(p \approx 10^{-8}\)), so we compared error models and chose ARMA(1,1) errors, which have the lowest AIC and BIC. The final model’s residuals pass the Ljung–Box test (\(p = 0.075\)). We then chose the regressors by forward selection on AIC under those errors. The selected model has one annual harmonic pair, the lockdown, a year-end shutdown indicator, the number of public holidays, planned outages and a quadratic in temperature. Selecting the regressors with ordinary least squares instead would also have added unplanned and other outages, which the error model shows are not needed. We estimated the model by maximum likelihood, by my own conditional sum of squares with optim() and by generalised least squares, and the estimates agree closely.
Demand is about 3,600 MW lower in the lockdown weeks, about 1,900 MW lower in the year-end shutdown, and about 260 MW lower for each public holiday in the week. Every 1,000 MW of planned outages goes with about 170 MW less peak demand. Temperature has a strong effect on the cold side: a week at 16 degrees (Celsius) has a peak about 2,300 MW higher than a week at 27 degrees, while a GAM check shows no clear increase in hot weeks. Allowing for autocorrelated errors widened the standard errors of the slowly varying terms (the seasonal cycle and the lockdown) and narrowed those of the terms that change week to week (holidays, temperature, year-end). The ARMA errors did not improve the forecasts. On the 12 test weeks the regression with independent errors has an RMSE of 875 MW, and over 11 rolling 12-week windows it has the lowest average error of my models (574 MW), well ahead of the seasonal naive model (1,037 MW) and a seasonal ARIMA model of the Project 1 type (1,116 MW).
If we were to do this again we would use measured station temperatures instead of reanalysis, forecast the outages and temperature instead of using their actual values, and test a daily model with day-of-week effects. A full detailed analysis follows below.
crumbs: 11  Project 3: Explaining and forecasting Eskom weekly peak demand with time series regression

title: 11  Project 3: Explaining and forecasting Eskom weekly peak demand with time series regression
text:
11.2 Data and EDA

11.2.1 Downloading and checking the data
The hourly data come from Eskom’s system data file, ESK6816.csv, which covers 1 April 2019 to 13 September 2023. We first checked that every day is complete, because a gap in a time series breaks lags, seasonality and the ACF. Table 11.1 below shows the check.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(here)
library(forecast)
library(nlme)
library(jsonlite)

file_path <- here("data", "ESK6816.csv")
if (!file.exists(file_path)) {
  stop("ESK6816.csv is not in the data folder. Download it from Amathuba (see Code and data).")
}

data <- read.csv(file_path) |>
  mutate(Date = as_date(ymd_hm(Date.Time.Hour.Beginning, tz = "Africa/Johannesburg"))) |>
  dplyr::select(Date, RSA.Contracted.Demand, RSA.Contracted.Forecast,
                Total.UCLF, Total.PCLF, Total.OCLF) |>
  filter(!is.na(RSA.Contracted.Demand))

daily <- data |>
  group_by(Date) |>
  summarise(peak = max(RSA.Contracted.Demand),
            hours = n(),
            .groups = "drop")

weekly_all <- data |>
  mutate(Week = floor_date(Date, "week", week_start = 1)) |>
  group_by(Week) |>
  summarise(peak = max(RSA.Contracted.Demand),
            esk_fc = max(RSA.Contracted.Forecast),
            uclf = mean(Total.UCLF, na.rm = TRUE),
            pclf = mean(Total.PCLF, na.rm = TRUE),
            oclf = mean(Total.OCLF, na.rm = TRUE),
            days = n_distinct(Date),
            .groups = "drop")

weekly <- weekly_all |> filter(days == 7)




Code
data.frame(first_day = min(daily$Date),
           last_day = max(daily$Date),
           days = nrow(daily),
           short_days = sum(daily$hours < 24),
           partial_weeks_dropped = nrow(weekly_all) - nrow(weekly))




Table 11.1: Completeness check of the daily series: first and last day, number of days, days with fewer than 24 hourly records, and the number of partial weeks dropped.







first_day
last_day
days
short_days
partial_weeks_dropped




2019-04-01
2023-09-13
1627
0
1









The series has 1,627 consecutive days, each with 24 hourly records, so no day needed to be dropped or filled. The last partial week (three days, starting 11 September 2023) was dropped, so every weekly maximum uses seven days. This leaves 232 weeks.


11.2.2 Choosing the time scale
The target is the weekly maximum of hourly demand. We chose the week over the day for two reasons. A weekly series is less noisy, so the annual, outage and temperature patterns are easier to see, and it matches the weekly target of Project 1, so the two projects use the same series. We used the maximum rather than the total because the peak is what the system has to be able to supply in its worst hour. Figure 11.1 below shows what the weekly scale loses compared to a daily scale.


Code
daily |>
  filter(Date >= as.Date("2021-01-04"), Date <= as.Date("2021-03-14")) |>
  ggplot(aes(Date, peak)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 week", date_labels = "%d %b") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Daily peak demand (MW)") +
  theme_minimal()








Figure 11.1: Daily peak RSA contracted demand (MW) for the first 10 weeks of 2021. Weekend days are clearly lower, so a daily model would need day-of-week terms.





The weekend dips in Figure 11.1 are a day-of-week pattern that a daily model would need its own terms for. Taking the weekly maximum removes it, because the maximum almost always falls on a weekday. This project is only concerned with maximum hourly demand per week.


11.2.3 Weather data
Electricity demand depends on the weather, and the Eskom file has no weather variables. We downloaded daily maximum temperatures for Johannesburg, Pretoria and Durban, the three largest load centres, from the Open-Meteo historical archive. These are modelled reanalysis values, not station measurements. We averaged the three cities each day and then took the weekly mean. The results are saved so it was only downloaded once and the analysis does not change if the archive is updated.


Code
temp_file <- here("data", "temp3_weekly.csv")
if (!file.exists(temp_file)) {
  base_url <- "https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive?start_date=2019-04-01&end_date=2023-09-13&daily=temperature_2m_max&timezone=Africa%2FJohannesburg"
  jhb <- fromJSON(paste0(base_url, "&latitude=-26.20&longitude=28.05"))$daily
  pta <- fromJSON(paste0(base_url, "&latitude=-25.75&longitude=28.19"))$daily
  dbn <- fromJSON(paste0(base_url, "&latitude=-29.86&longitude=31.03"))$daily

  temp_daily <- data.frame(Date = as.Date(jhb$time),
                           tmax = (jhb$temperature_2m_max + pta$temperature_2m_max + dbn$temperature_2m_max) / 3)
  temp_wk <- temp_daily |>
    mutate(Week = floor_date(Date, "week", week_start = 1)) |>
    group_by(Week) |>
    summarise(temp3 = mean(tmax), .groups = "drop")
  write.csv(temp_wk, temp_file, row.names = FALSE)
}

temp_wk <- read.csv(temp_file) |> mutate(Week = as.Date(Week))
weekly <- weekly |> left_join(temp_wk, by = "Week")




11.2.4 Exploring the weekly series
Figure 11.2 shows the weekly target together with the outage and temperature series (in degrees Celsius).


Code
weekly |>
  dplyr::select(Week, peak, pclf, uclf, temp3) |>
  pivot_longer(-Week, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = c("peak", "pclf", "uclf", "temp3"),
                           labels = c("Weekly peak demand (MW)", "Planned outages, PCLF (MW)",
                                      "Unplanned outages, UCLF (MW)", "Temperature (degrees)"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(Week, value)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()








Figure 11.2: Weekly peak RSA contracted demand, weekly average planned (PCLF) and unplanned (UCLF) outages (all MW), and weekly mean of the daily maximum temperature in Johannesburg, Pretoria and Durban (degrees), April 2019 to September 2023.





Demand has a clear annual cycle, peaking in the southern winter and dipping sharply at the turn of each year. It also falls in April 2020, during the hard lockdown of COVID-19. Temperature moves almost exactly opposite to demand, which suggests that cold weather drives the winter peak. Planned outages are also high when demand is low, which fits maintenance being scheduled for quieter periods. Unplanned outages trend upwards over the whole period while demand does not, so they look unlikely to explain much.

title: 11  Project 3: Explaining and forecasting Eskom weekly peak demand with time series regression
text:
11.3 Building the regression

11.3.1 Candidate regressors
we chose all candidates before looking at the test weeks, and every choice in this section uses only the first 220 weeks. Thermal generation, imports and exports and Eskom’s own demand forecast were not considered as regressors, as generation and trade respond to demand rather than drive it, and the forecast would make the regression circular. The candidates are as follows:

Annual harmonics: \(s_{k,t} = \sin(2\pi k t / 52.18)\) and \(c_{k,t} = \cos(2\pi k t / 52.18)\), where \(t\) counts weeks and 52.18 = 365.25/7 is the length of a year in weeks.
Lockdown: 1 for the weeks starting 30 March to 27 April 2020 (the hard lockdown), 0 otherwise.
Year-end: 1 for weeks starting between 22 December and 6 January, when much of industry shuts down.
Public holidays: the number of public holidays in the week. The dates were typed in from the official calendar.
Outages: the weekly averages of planned (PCLF), unplanned (UCLF) and other (OCLF) outages.
Temperature: the weekly temperature and its square, so that demand can rise for both cold and hot weeks.



Code
sa_hol <- as_date(c(
  "2019-01-01", "2019-03-21", "2019-04-19", "2019-04-22", "2019-04-27", "2019-05-01", "2019-06-16", "2019-08-09", "2019-09-24", "2019-12-16", "2019-12-25", "2019-12-26",
  "2020-01-01", "2020-03-21", "2020-04-10", "2020-04-13", "2020-04-27", "2020-05-01", "2020-06-16", "2020-08-10", "2020-09-24", "2020-12-16", "2020-12-25", "2020-12-26",
  "2021-01-01", "2021-03-21", "2021-04-02", "2021-04-05", "2021-04-27", "2021-05-01", "2021-06-16", "2021-08-09", "2021-09-24", "2021-12-16", "2021-12-25", "2021-12-26",
  "2022-01-01", "2022-03-21", "2022-04-15", "2022-04-18", "2022-04-27", "2022-05-02", "2022-06-16", "2022-08-09", "2022-09-24", "2022-12-16", "2022-12-26",
  "2023-01-02", "2023-03-21", "2023-04-07", "2023-04-10", "2023-04-27", "2023-05-01", "2023-06-16", "2023-08-09", "2023-09-24", "2023-12-16", "2023-12-25", "2023-12-26"))

period <- 365.25 / 7

weekly <- weekly |>
  mutate(t = row_number(),
         lockdown = as.numeric(Week >= as.Date("2020-03-30") & Week <= as.Date("2020-04-27")),
         yearend = as.numeric(format(Week, "%m-%d") >= "12-22" | format(Week, "%m-%d") <= "01-06"),
         hol_count = rowSums(outer(as.numeric(Week), as.numeric(sa_hol), "<=") &
                             outer(as.numeric(Week) + 6, as.numeric(sa_hol), ">=")),
         s1 = sin(2 * pi * t / period),
         c1 = cos(2 * pi * t / period),
         temp_sq = temp3^2)

train <- weekly |> slice(1:(n() - 12))
test <- weekly |> slice((n() - 11):n())

cands <- c("yearend", "hol_count", "pclf", "uclf", "oclf", "temp3", "temp_sq")
all_vars <- c("s1", "c1", "lockdown", cands)


Table 11.2 confirms that the lockdown dummy is used only in 2020. It is a temporary intervention, which is not the same as a structural break, so it cannot describe a lasting change in demand.

Code
table(weekly$lockdown, lubridate::year(weekly$Week))




Table 11.2: Number of weeks coded as lockdown (1) and not (0), by year, over the whole series.



   
    2019 2020 2021 2022 2023
  0   40   47   52   52   36
  1    0    5    0    0    0




The training weeks contain 9 year-end weeks and 46 weeks with at least one public holiday. Their temperatures range from 16.0 degrees to 29.7 degrees. Table 11.3 shows how each candidate relates to demand on the training weeks, both in levels and after first differencing. Differencing removes most of the shared seasonal pattern, so the differenced column shows whether the week-to-week movements agree.


Code
check_vars <- c("pclf", "uclf", "oclf", "hol_count", "temp3")
data.frame(variable = check_vars,
           cor_level = sapply(check_vars, function(v) cor(train$peak, train[[v]])),
           cor_diff = sapply(check_vars, function(v) cor(diff(train$peak), diff(train[[v]]))),
           row.names = NULL) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2)))

11.3.2 Do the errors need a model?
Before choosing the regressors, we checked whether the regression errors are independent. If they are not, the OLS standard errors and AIC values are too optimistic, and an AIC-based choice of regressors tends to keep terms that only fit the autocorrelated noise. We fitted OLS with every candidate and looked at the residuals in Figure 11.3 below.


Code
ols_all <- lm(reformulate(all_vars, "peak"), data = train)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
acf(resid(ols_all), lag.max = 30, main = "ACF of OLS residuals")
pacf(resid(ols_all), lag.max = 30, main = "PACF of OLS residuals")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))








Figure 11.3: Sample ACF and PACF of the residuals from the OLS regression with all candidate regressors, training weeks, up to lag 30.





The ACF in Figure 11.3 above decays slowly, from 0.31 at lag 1 to about 0.22 at lag 4, and the PACF has significant spikes at lags 1 to 3 (0.31, 0.16 and 0.16). A slowly decaying ACF with a PACF that does not cut off cleanly points to an ARMA model rather than a simple low-order AR. Table 11.4 below compares the possible error models for the same regressors, using AIC, BIC, and a Ljung-Box test.


Code
orders <- list(c(0, 0, 0), c(1, 0, 0), c(2, 0, 0), c(1, 0, 1), c(2, 0, 1), c(1, 0, 2))
err_tab <- data.frame()
for (o in orders) {
  fa <- Arima(train$peak, order = o, xreg = as.matrix(train[, all_vars]))
  err_tab <- rbind(err_tab,
                   data.frame(errors = paste0("ARMA(", o[1], ",", o[3], ")"),
                              AIC = AIC(fa),
                              BIC = BIC(fa),
                              LB_p = Box.test(resid(fa), lag = 20, type = "Ljung-Box",
                                              fitdf = o[1] + o[3])$p.value))
}
err_tab |>
  mutate(across(c(AIC, BIC), ~ round(.x, 1)),
         LB_p = signif(LB_p, 2))

Independent errors, the ARMA(0,0), are clearly rejected (\(p \approx 10^{-8}\)). AR(1) errors remove most of the autocorrelation but still fail the Ljung–Box test (\(p = 0.002\)), and AR(2) fails as well (\(p = 0.015\)). ARMA(1,1) has the lowest AIC (3,463.8) and the lowest BIC (3,511.3) and passes the test (\(p = 0.084\)). The two larger models do not improve on it. We therefore used the ARMA(1,1) errors,
\[y_t = x_t'\beta + u_t, \qquad u_t = \phi u_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t + \theta \varepsilon_{t-1}, \qquad \varepsilon_t \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2),\]
where \(x_t\) holds the regressors and \(u_t\) is the regression error.


11.3.3 Choosing the regressors
We then chose the regressors by forward selection on AIC, starting from the annual cycle and the lockdown. At each step we added the candidate that lowered the AIC the most, and stopped when no candidate lowered it further. Every model in this search has ARMA(1,1) errors. Table 11.5 shows the path and which variable that was added at each step, and the resulting AIC.


Code
cur <- c("s1", "c1", "lockdown")
left <- cands
path_arma <- data.frame(step = 0, added = "start: s1, c1, lockdown",
                        AIC = AIC(Arima(train$peak, order = c(1, 0, 1), xreg = as.matrix(train[, cur]))))
repeat {
  aics <- c()
  for (v in left) {
    aics[v] <- AIC(Arima(train$peak, order = c(1, 0, 1), xreg = as.matrix(train[, c(cur, v)])))
  }
  if (min(aics) >= tail(path_arma$AIC, 1)) break
  best_v <- names(which.min(aics))
  cur <- c(cur, best_v)
  left <- setdiff(left, best_v)
  path_arma <- rbind(path_arma, data.frame(step = nrow(path_arma), added = best_v, AIC = min(aics)))
  if (length(left) == 0) break
}
final_vars <- cur

path_arma |> mutate(AIC = round(AIC, 1))

11.4 Final model
The final regression is fitted to the training weeks by maximum likelihood with ARMA(1,1) errors. Table 11.8 compares its estimates with the same regression fitted by OLS, which assumes independent errors.


Code
X_train <- as.matrix(train[, final_vars])
X_test <- as.matrix(test[, final_vars])

ols <- lm(reformulate(final_vars, "peak"), data = train)
fit_arma <- Arima(train$peak, order = c(1, 0, 1), xreg = X_train)
se_arma <- sqrt(diag(vcov(fit_arma)))

data.frame(term = c("(Intercept)", final_vars, "ar1 (phi)", "ma1 (theta)"),
           ols_est = c(coef(ols), NA, NA),
           ols_se = c(summary(ols)$coefficients[, 2], NA, NA),
           arma_est = coef(fit_arma)[c("intercept", final_vars, "ar1", "ma1")],
           arma_se = se_arma[c("intercept", final_vars, "ar1", "ma1")],
           row.names = NULL) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))

With the ARMA(1,1) estimates from Table 11.8, the fitted model is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat y_t &= 46\,451 + 1\,069.2\, s_{1,t} - 192.4\, c_{1,t} - 3\,608.2\, L_t \\
&\quad - 1\,875.2\, Y_t - 258.1\, H_t - 0.172\, P_t - 1\,100.8\, T_t + 20.67\, T_t^2
\end{aligned}
\]
\[u_t = 0.896\, u_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t - 0.560\, \varepsilon_{t-1}, \qquad \hat\sigma^2 = 373\,237,\]
where \(L_t\) is the lockdown dummy, \(Y_t\) the year-end indicator, \(H_t\) the number of public holidays, \(P_t\) planned outages (MW) and \(T_t\) temperature (degrees).
The coefficients read as follows, holding the other terms fixed.

Lockdown: the peak was about 3,600 MW lower in the five hard-lockdown weeks.
Year-end: the peak is about 1,900 MW lower in the shutdown weeks.
Holidays: each public holiday in a week lowers the weekly peak by about 260 MW.
Planned outages: each extra 1,000 MW of planned outages goes with about 170 MW less peak demand. This is an association rather than a causal effect, because maintenance is scheduled for weeks when demand is expected to be low.
Annual cycle: the sine and cosine terms give an annual swing of about \(\sqrt{1069^2 + 192^2} \approx 1{,}090\) MW on top of the temperature effect.

The intercept is large because it is the value at 0 degrees, far outside the data, so it has no direct meaning. The error terms show that a demand shock decays slowly (\(\hat\phi = 0.90\)), but about half of each new shock is cancelled in the following week (\(\hat\theta = -0.56\)).
Temperature enters as a curve, so its effect is easier to read from a plot. Figure 11.4 shows the effect of temperature relative to its minimum.


Code
b_t <- coef(fit_arma)[["temp3"]]
b_t2 <- coef(fit_arma)[["temp_sq"]]
t_min <- -b_t / (2 * b_t2)

data.frame(temp = seq(15, 30, by = 0.1)) |>
  mutate(effect = b_t * temp + b_t2 * temp^2 - (b_t * t_min + b_t2 * t_min^2)) |>
  ggplot(aes(temp, effect)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_rug(data = train, aes(x = temp3), inherit.aes = FALSE, sides = "b", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Weekly temperature (degrees)", y = "Effect on weekly peak (MW)") +
  theme_minimal()

Demand is lowest at about 26.6 degrees. A week averaging 20 degrees has a peak about 900 MW higher, and a week averaging 16 degrees, the coldest in the data, about 2,300 MW higher.

11.4.1 Checking the temperature curve with a GAM
The slides fit electricity demand with a generalised additive model (GAM) with correlated errors, where each effect can be a smooth curve estimated from the data. We refitted the final model with a smooth function of temperature, \(f(T_t)\), in place of the quadratic, keeping the ARMA(1,1) errors. Table 11.9 gives the smooth term, and Figure 11.5 compares the two temperature curves.


Code
library(mgcv)
fit_gamm <- gamm(peak ~ s1 + c1 + lockdown + yearend + hol_count + pclf + s(temp3),
                 data = train, correlation = corARMA(p = 1, q = 1))

summary(fit_gamm$gam)$s.table |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("term") |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ signif(.x, 3)))

quad <- b_t * temp_grid + b_t2 * temp_grid^2
quad_mean <- mean(b_t * train$temp3 + b_t2 * train$temp3^2)

     xlab = "Weekly temperature (degrees)", ylab = "Effect on weekly peak (MW)", main = "")

Figure 11.5: Estimated effect of weekly temperature on weekly peak demand: the GAM smooth (black) with its 95% band (dashed) and the quadratic from the final model (red), both centred to average zero over the training weeks.





The smooth temperature term has 3.8 effective degrees of freedom (Table 11.9), somewhat more than the two of a quadratic, and it is clearly significant (p < 0.001). In Figure 11.5 the two curves agree closely below about 24 degrees: demand falls steeply as temperature rises, by roughly 2,000 MW between the coldest weeks and 22 degrees. Above about 25 degrees they differ in shape. The smooth flattens out and keeps falling slightly, while the quadratic turns upwards at the hot end. The quadratic stays inside the 95% band of the smooth across the whole range, so the data do not reject it. However, the GAM gives no evidence of the hot-weather increase that the quadratic implies. The upturn in the final model is probably a consequence of forcing a symmetric U shape, rather than an air-conditioning effect, which fits the hot side resting on only 38 training weeks. We will keep the quadratic in the final model because it is simpler to interpret and to write as an equation, but we would not claim from this model that demand rises in hot weeks.


11.4.2 What the error model changes
Comparing the standard errors in Table 11.8 shows what the error model changes. Its standard errors are larger for the slowly varying terms. The first sine term rises from 129 to 194 and the lockdown from 354 to 415. The cosine term is significant under OLS (\(t \approx -2.7\)) but not with ARMA errors (\(t \approx -1.2\)). The standard errors are smaller for the terms that change from one week to the next: the holiday count falls from 110 to 84, the year-end indicator from 270 to 228 and the temperature terms from 245 to 210 and from 5.2 to 4.4.
This makes sense, as with autocorrelated errors, a smooth regressor such as the seasonal cycle is hard to separate from a slowly wandering error, so its effect is less certain than OLS suggests. A regressor that jumps from week to week, such as a holiday, can be separated from the error much better once the error is modelled, because the model compares each week with what the error was expected to be. So OLS is overconfident about the seasonal terms and under confident about the calendar and temperature terms. The point estimates move much less than the standard errors, apart from the lockdown, which falls from about −4,530 MW to −3,610 MW. Under OLS, part of the lockdown dip was explained by the dummy. With ARMA errors, the slowly decaying error absorbs some of the weeks around it.


11.4.3 Residual diagnostics
Figure 11.6 below checks the residuals of the final model.


Code
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(train$Week, resid(fit_arma), type = "h", xlab = "", ylab = "Residual (MW)",
     main = "Residuals over time")
abline(h = 0, col = "grey")
acf(resid(fit_arma), lag.max = 30, main = "ACF of residuals")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))








Figure 11.6: Residuals of the final regression with ARMA(1,1) errors over the training weeks (left) and their sample ACF (right).





The residuals in Figure 11.6 have no obvious pattern over time, and the ACF has only isolated spikes, about as many as chance would give over 30 lags. The Ljung–Box test over 20 lags gives \(p = 0.075\), so there is no significant autocorrelation left. The residual standard deviation is about 600 MW, against 729 MW for the OLS fit.

title: 11  Project 3: Explaining and forecasting Eskom weekly peak demand with time series regression
text:
11.5 Estimation from first principles
The notes describe estimating a regression with ARMA errors by minimising the sum of squares of the independent errors. For ARMA(1,1) errors, we first compute the regression errors \(u_t = y_t - x_t'\beta\). The independent errors then follow recursively,
\[\varepsilon_t = u_t - \phi u_{t-1} - \theta \varepsilon_{t-1}, \qquad t = 2, \dots, n,\]
starting from \(\varepsilon_1 = 0\). We minimised \(\sum_{t=2}^{n} \varepsilon_t^2\) over \(\beta\), \(\phi\) and \(\theta\) with optim(), starting from the OLS estimates, \(\phi = 0.5\) and \(\theta = 0\). This is the conditional sum of squares, which Arima() also offers with method = "CSS", so the two can be compared exactly. Table 11.10 below also includes the maximum likelihood fit and generalised least squares with an ARMA(1,1) correlation structure from nlme.


Code
y <- train$peak
X <- cbind(1, X_train)
n_b <- ncol(X)

css_arma11 <- function(par) {
  beta <- par[1:n_b]
  phi <- par[n_b + 1]
  theta <- par[n_b + 2]
  u <- y - as.numeric(X %*% beta)
  e <- numeric(length(y))
  for (t in 2:length(y)) {
    e[t] <- u[t] - phi * u[t - 1] - theta * e[t - 1]
  }
  sum(e[-1]^2)
}

fit_own <- optim(c(coef(ols), 0.5, 0), css_arma11, method = "BFGS",
                 control = list(parscale = c(summary(ols)$coefficients[, 2], 0.1, 0.1),
                                maxit = 5000))
fit_css <- Arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 1), xreg = X_train, method = "CSS")
fit_gls <- gls(reformulate(final_vars, "peak"), data = train,
               correlation = corARMA(p = 1, q = 1))

data.frame(term = c("(Intercept)", final_vars, "phi", "theta"),
           own_css = fit_own$par,
           arima_css = coef(fit_css)[c("intercept", final_vars, "ar1", "ma1")],
           arima_ml = coef(fit_arma)[c("intercept", final_vars, "ar1", "ma1")],
           gls = c(coef(fit_gls), coef(fit_gls$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)),
           row.names = NULL) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))

title: 11  Project 3: Explaining and forecasting Eskom weekly peak demand with time series regression
text:
11.6 Forecasts for the 12 held-out weeks
For the 12 test weeks, the harmonic, lockdown, year-end and holiday terms are known in advance, but planned outages and temperature are not. We used their actual values, so this test measures how well the model works if outages and temperature were known, not how it would forecast them in reality. The the outages would be at least partly planned ahead and a weather forecast is available a week or two out.
For the regression with ARMA(1,1) errors, the forecast is the regression part plus the forecast of the error. At the end of the training data, \(\hat u_n\) and \(\hat\varepsilon_n\) are known, so the next error is forecast as \(\hat u_{n+1} = \hat\phi \hat u_n + \hat\theta \hat\varepsilon_n\). After that the shocks are forecast as zero, so \(\hat u_{n+h} = \hat\phi^{\,h-1} \hat u_{n+1}\). We compute this from my our estimates and compared it with forecast() in Table 11.11 below. which compares the errors, the coverage of the 95% prediction intervals and their average width.


Code
p_ols <- predict(ols, newdata = test, interval = "prediction", level = 0.95)
p_arma <- forecast(fit_arma, xreg = X_test, level = 95)

b_own <- fit_own$par[1:n_b]
phi_own <- fit_own$par[n_b + 1]
theta_own <- fit_own$par[n_b + 2]
u_own <- y - as.numeric(X %*% b_own)
e_own <- numeric(length(y))
for (t in 2:length(y)) {
  e_own[t] <- u_own[t] - phi_own * u_own[t - 1] - theta_own * e_own[t - 1]
}
u_next <- phi_own * tail(u_own, 1) + theta_own * tail(e_own, 1)
fc_own <- as.numeric(cbind(1, X_test) %*% b_own) + u_next * phi_own^(0:(nrow(test) - 1))

fc_ols <- as.numeric(p_ols[, "fit"])
fc_arma <- as.numeric(p_arma$mean)

data.frame(model = c("OLS", "ARMA(1,1) errors", "ARMA(1,1) errors, own"),
           RMSE = c(sqrt(mean((test$peak - fc_ols)^2)),
                    sqrt(mean((test$peak - fc_arma)^2)),
                    sqrt(mean((test$peak - fc_own)^2))),
           MAE = c(mean(abs(test$peak - fc_ols)),
                   mean(abs(test$peak - fc_arma)),
                   mean(abs(test$peak - fc_own))),
           inside_95 = c(sum(test$peak >= p_ols[, "lwr"] & test$peak <= p_ols[, "upr"]),
                         sum(test$peak >= p_arma$lower[, 1] & test$peak <= p_arma$upper[, 1]),
                         NA),
           width = c(mean(p_ols[, "upr"] - p_ols[, "lwr"]),
                     mean(p_arma$upper[, 1] - p_arma$lower[, 1]),
                     NA)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 0)))
