title: 11  Project 3: Explaining and forecasting Eskom weekly peak demand with time series regression
text:
11.7 Rolling-origin evaluation
One 12-week window is a small sample, so we repeated the forecasts from 11 origins, 12 weeks apart. At each origin both models are refitted on the data up to that week and forecast the next 12. The first origin is week 100, so the lockdown is always in the training data. The regressors and error model are kept as chosen above. Table 11.12 below summarises the results.


Code
origins <- seq(100, nrow(weekly) - 12, by = 12)
err_o <- c()
err_a <- c()
in_o <- 0
in_a <- 0

for (k in origins) {
  tr <- weekly[1:k, ]
  te <- weekly[(k + 1):(k + 12), ]

  f_o <- lm(reformulate(final_vars, "peak"), data = tr)
  f_a <- Arima(tr$peak, order = c(1, 0, 1), xreg = as.matrix(tr[, final_vars]))
  p_o <- predict(f_o, newdata = te, interval = "prediction", level = 0.95)
  p_a <- forecast(f_a, xreg = as.matrix(te[, final_vars]), level = 95)

  err_o <- rbind(err_o, te$peak - p_o[, "fit"])
  err_a <- rbind(err_a, te$peak - as.numeric(p_a$mean))
  in_o <- in_o + sum(te$peak >= p_o[, "lwr"] & te$peak <= p_o[, "upr"])
  in_a <- in_a + sum(te$peak >= p_a$lower[, 1] & te$peak <= p_a$upper[, 1])
}

rmse_o <- sqrt(rowMeans(err_o^2))
rmse_a <- sqrt(rowMeans(err_a^2))

data.frame(model = c("OLS", "ARMA(1,1) errors"),
           mean_RMSE = c(mean(rmse_o), mean(rmse_a)),
           windows_won = c(sum(rmse_o < rmse_a), sum(rmse_a < rmse_o)),
           coverage = c(in_o, in_a) / length(err_o)) |>
  mutate(across(c(mean_RMSE, windows_won), ~ round(.x, 0)),
         coverage = round(coverage, 3))




Table 11.12: Rolling-origin evaluation of the final regression with independent errors and with ARMA(1,1) errors over 11 origins: average 12-week RMSE (MW), number of windows with the lower RMSE, and the share of the 132 forecast weeks inside the 95% prediction interval.

Across the 11 windows the regression with independent errors forecasts better. Its average RMSE is 574 MW against 641 MW, and it wins 9 of the 11 windows. Both sets of prediction intervals are slightly conservative: 98.5% (OLS) and 96.2% (ARMA) of the 132 forecast weeks fall inside the nominal 95% intervals. Figure 11.8 shows how the error depends on how far ahead the forecast is.


Code
data.frame(h = 1:12,
           OLS = sqrt(colMeans(err_o^2)),
           ARMA_errors = sqrt(colMeans(err_a^2))) |>
  pivot_longer(-h, names_to = "model", values_to = "RMSE") |>
  ggplot(aes(h, RMSE, colour = model)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(OLS = "darkgreen", ARMA_errors = "red")) +
  labs(x = "Weeks ahead", y = "RMSE (MW)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()








Figure 11.8: Rolling-origin RMSE by forecast horizon for the final regression with independent errors and with ARMA(1,1) errors, over 11 origins.





The ARMA error term should help most at short horizons, where the last error still carries information. However, Figure 11.8 above does not show that, as the OLS is better at 10 of the 12 horizons, including one week ahead (491 against 523 MW). Each horizon rests on only 11 forecasts, so the curves are noisy. With \(\hat\phi\) close to 0.9 the error forecast decays slowly, so a large residual at the origin is carried into many forecast weeks, and that seems to hurt more often than it helps. The conclusion is that the error model matters for inference, and it does not improve the forecasts, the same as in the test window.
These windows are not fully out of sample. The regressors and error model were chosen on weeks 1 to 220, which includes the test weeks of the first 10 windows, so the rolling errors are probably slightly optimistic. Only the last window is fully independent of the model choice.

11.8 Fitted values over the whole series
Figure 11.9 shows the final regression fitted to all 232 weeks, which shows how much of the series the model explains, rather than how well it forecasts.


Code
ols_full <- lm(reformulate(final_vars, "peak"), data = weekly)

ggplot(weekly, aes(Week)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = peak), colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted(ols_full)), colour = "darkgreen", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Weekly peak demand (MW)") +
  theme_minimal()








Figure 11.9: Observed weekly peak demand (grey) and the fitted values of the final regression (OLS) fitted to all 232 weeks.





The fitted line in Figure 11.9 follows the winter peaks, the year-end dips and the lockdown, and it tracks a good part of the week-to-week movement through temperature and outages, except in 2019, where the fit is about 1,000 MW too low. On the training weeks the model explains about 84% of the variance in the weekly peak. What it misses is mostly short, sharp spikes, which the slowly decaying ARMA error describes but cannot predict.

text:
11.9 Comparison with benchmarks and Project 1
Finally, we compare the regression with two benchmarks.

Seasonal naive: the value 52 weeks earlier.
Seasonal ARIMA: a model of the Project 1 type, with period 52, chosen automatically on the training weeks. The chosen model is ARIMA(0,1,2)(1,1,0)[52].

Both use only the past demand, so they have no information about outages, temperature or the calendar. Table 11.13 compares the errors on the 12 test weeks.


Code
fc_snaive <- weekly$peak[test$t - 52]
fit_sarima <- auto.arima(ts(train$peak, frequency = 52))
fc_sarima <- as.numeric(forecast(fit_sarima, h = nrow(test))$mean)

err_b <- cbind(Regression_OLS = test$peak - fc_ols,
               Regression_ARMA = test$peak - fc_arma,
               Seasonal_naive = test$peak - fc_snaive,
               SARIMA = test$peak - fc_sarima)

data.frame(model = colnames(err_b),
           RMSE = sqrt(colMeans(err_b^2)),
           MAE = colMeans(abs(err_b)),
           row.names = NULL) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 0)))

Both are far ahead of seasonal naive (1,037 MW, 2 wins) and the seasonal ARIMA (1,116 MW, 2 wins). The two time series benchmarks do worst in the windows just after the lockdown, where they carry the lockdown dip into the following year. Figure 11.10 shows the same comparison by horizon.

           Regression_OLS = sqrt(colMeans(err_o^2)),

In Figure 11.10 the regression with independent errors stays between about 260 and 800 MW at every horizon, while the two time series benchmarks are at about 780 to 1,800 MW. The regression’s advantage does not fade with the horizon, because most of its information comes from the calendar, temperature and outages rather than from recent demand.
This changes the comparison with Project 1. A seasonal ARIMA on weekly peaks has to learn the annual shape from one or two past years, which includes a lockdown and shifting year-end weeks. The regression is told about these directly, so it forecasts much better. Figure 11.11 shows how closely each model follows the observed weekly peaks over the whole series.


Code

  dplyr::select(Week, peak, Regression_OLS, Regression_ARMA, Seasonal_naive, SARIMA) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(Week, peak), names_to = "model", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = c("Regression_OLS", "Regression_ARMA", "Seasonal_naive", "SARIMA"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(Week)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = peak), colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = value, colour = model), linewidth = 0.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~model, ncol = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Regression_OLS = "darkgreen", Regression_ARMA = "red",
                                 Seasonal_naive = "orange", SARIMA = "blue")) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Weekly peak demand (MW)") +
  guides(colour = "none") +
  theme_minimal()








Figure 11.11: Observed weekly peak demand (grey) and the values from the final regression with independent errors, the final regression with ARMA(1,1) errors (regression part only), seasonal naive (the value 52 weeks earlier) and the seasonal ARIMA (one-step-ahead fitted values), each fitted to all 232 weeks.





The two regression fits follow the year-end dips and the lockdown in the year they happen, and they are almost identical to each other. Seasonal naive repeats the previous year’s shape, so it misses the dip in 2020 and then repeats it in 2021, and it starts a year in because it needs 52 weeks of history. The seasonal ARIMA is a one-step-ahead fit, which uses the previous week’s observed value, so it tracks the data more closely than the other three and is not a fair comparison with them. The test tables above are the fair comparison. Figure 11.12 puts the regression and the seasonal ARIMA on the same axes.

weekly |>
  mutate(Regression_OLS = as.numeric(fitted(ols_full)),
         SARIMA = as.numeric(fitted(sarima_full))) |>
  ggplot(aes(Week)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = peak, colour = "Observed"), linewidth = 1.2, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Regression_OLS, colour = "Regression (OLS)"), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = SARIMA, colour = "SARIMA"), linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Observed" = "grey60", "Regression (OLS)" = "darkgreen",
                                 "SARIMA" = "blue")) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Weekly peak demand (MW)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 11.12: Observed weekly peak demand (grey) and the values from the final regression with independent errors (green) and the seasonal ARIMA, one-step-ahead (blue), each fitted to all 232 weeks.





The differences are hard to see on this scale, so Figure 11.13 below shows the errors of the two models instead.


Code
weekly |>
  mutate(Regression_OLS = peak - as.numeric(fitted(ols_full)),
         SARIMA = peak - as.numeric(fitted(sarima_full))) |>
  dplyr::select(Week, Regression_OLS, SARIMA) |>
  pivot_longer(-Week, names_to = "model", values_to = "error") |>
  ggplot(aes(Week, error, colour = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Regression_OLS = "darkgreen", SARIMA = "blue")) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Error (MW)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 11.13: Errors (observed minus fitted, MW) of the final regression with independent errors (green) and the seasonal ARIMA, one-step-ahead (blue), over the whole series. A line closer to zero is a better fit.





The regression’s errors are mostly within about plus minus 1,500 MW. The largest are the weeks just after the lockdown dummy ends in May 2020 (about −3,100 MW), because demand recovered more slowly than the model allows, and the first winter of 2019, where the model is too low. The seasonal ARIMA’s errors are exactly zero in the first year, only because the seasonal differencing has no earlier year to compare with. Its largest errors (about +4,900 MW in early 2021 and about +2,500 MW in early 2022) come from repeating the 2020 lockdown dip a year later, which is the weakness of a model that only looks at past demand.

title: 11  Project 3: Explaining and forecasting Eskom weekly peak demand with time series regression
text:
11.10 Limitations
The forecasts are not true forecasts. They use the actual planned outages and temperatures of the forecast weeks. A usable forecast would need outage plans and a weather forecast, and the errors would be larger.
The temperature is a proxy. It is modelled reanalysis for three cities, not measured national demand-weighted temperature. The hot side of the curve rests on 38 training weeks, and the GAM check finds no evidence that demand rises in hot weeks.
Planned outages are not a cause. Maintenance is scheduled around expected demand, so the PCLF coefficient describes when maintenance happens rather than what it does to demand. Load-shedding also suppresses observed demand, so in some weeks the series is supply rather than true demand, and no term in the model accounts for this.
The evidence for some terms is thin. The lockdown dummy rests on 5 weeks and the year-end indicator on 9. The holiday dates were typed in by hand.
The rolling evaluation overlaps the model choice. The regressors and the error model were chosen on weeks 1 to 220, which includes the test weeks of the first 10 rolling windows.
The model is weekly. A daily model would need day-of-week terms and a more complex error model, and could forecast at the horizons Eskom works at.
crumbs: 11  Project 3: Explaining and forecasting Eskom weekly peak demand with time series regression

title: 11  Project 3: Explaining and forecasting Eskom weekly peak demand with time series regression
text:
11.11 Reflection
The most important thing we learned in this project is that the error model has to come before the choice of regressors. In my first version we chose the regressors with ordinary least squares and only then looked at the residuals. When we chose the error model first, the forward selection dropped unplanned and other outages, which OLS had kept. Temperature, which had looked useless as a straight line, became one of the strongest terms once we let it be a curve. The OLS search had kept extra terms because autocorrelated errors make every extra term look more useful than it is.
I was surprised that modelling the errors did not make the standard errors larger across the board. They grew for the seasonal terms and the lockdown, and they shrank for the holidays, year-end and temperature. It took me a while to see that a smooth regressor is hard to separate from a slowly wandering error, while a regressor that jumps from week to week is easier to separate once the error is modelled.
Writing my own conditional sum of squares for ARMA(1,1) errors made the model concrete for me. The notes give the AR(1) case. Working out the recursion with the extra \(\theta \varepsilon_{t-1}\) term, and then getting the same numbers as Arima(method = "CSS"), showed me exactly what the package does. It also explained why the maximum likelihood estimates differ slightly.
we also checked the temperature curve with a GAM, which let the data choose the shape. It agreed with the quadratic on the cold side but found no evidence of the increase in demand in hot weeks that the quadratic implies, so we would not claim that from this model.
The forecasting results changed how we think about the error model. On the single test window the seasonal ARIMA first looked best. Across 11 rolling windows the regression was clearly better than both time series benchmarks, and the regression with independent errors forecast better than the one with ARMA errors. So the error model is about honest inference, not better forecasts, and one test window can give the wrong ranking.
This project changed my perception of time series regression. We had expected it to look much more like a regular regression problem, with the ARMA errors being the only “time” component. This wasn’t the case, because most of my regressors are functions of the calendar (the seasonal cycle, the lockdown, the year-end and the holidays), and only the outages and temperature are measured series. We would be interested to see how this differs with a data set that has many more measured explanatory variables, to see whether the calendar terms are still needed. We now have a much better understanding of the kinds of regressors that get used with time series data, as we had little prior experience with this kind of data. Even the temperature variable took me time to figure out. We had not considered that its relationship with demand could be curved, and it did not improve the model until we added the squared term.

title: 12  Project 4: Kalman filter simulation study
text:
12.1 Summary
Kalman filter simulation study (Part 2, state space models and the Kalman filter; implementation project; covers computational / statistical programming).
This project asks whether my own Kalman filter, written from first principles, can recover the hidden state of a simulated state space model and estimate its two error variances. It is based on tutorial Question 1 and Meinhold and Singpurwalla (1983). I simulated 100 observations from \(y_t = F_t\theta_t + v_t\) and \(\theta_t = G_t\theta_{t-1} + w_t\), with \(V = 2\), \(W = 1\), \(G_t = (-1)^t/2\) and \(F_t \sim N(1, 0.2^2)\), using set.seed(1997). I coded the filter by hand, first for one observation and then as a loop, and wrapped it in a function that returns the negative log-likelihood from the prediction error decomposition. I estimated \(V\) and \(W\) by maximum likelihood with optim() on the log scale, made 5-step forecasts with prediction intervals by treating future observations as missing, and checked the standardised residuals with an ACF plot and a Ljung–Box test.
The filtered state follows the turning points of the true state but is smoother and misses the extremes. The maximum likelihood estimates are \(\hat V = 1.58\) and \(\hat W = 1.39\), against the true values of 2 and 1, with a negative log-likelihood of 105.915 compared with 106.158 at the true values. The total noise is about right, but it is split differently between the two equations, which matches the slides’ warning that the variances can be hard to separate. The forecasts decay quickly towards zero because each step multiplies by ±0.5, and the prediction intervals are wide. The standardised residuals show no significant autocorrelation, so the filter has captured the dependence in the data.
If I did this again, I would first check my filter against Table 1 of Meinhold and Singpurwalla (1983), repeat the simulation many times to see whether the variance estimates are biased or just vary from sample to sample, and try several starting values for optim(). A full detailed analysis follows below.
crumbs: 12  Project 4: Kalman filter simulation study

title: 12  Project 4: Kalman filter simulation study
text:
12.2 Analysis

12.2.1 Q1 - Simulating Data
First we set starting values and a seed for reproducibility.


Code
set.seed(1997)
n <- 100
V <- 2
W <- 1


Then we define functions for each part of the Kalman Filter. The plot below also helped confirm the expected cyclical behaviour.


Code
func_Gt <- function(t) {
  ((-1)^t)/2
}

plot(func_Gt(1:10),type = "l")









Then we define functions for Theta, W amd V.


Code
func_wt <- function(W){
  rnorm(1,0,sqrt(W))
}

func_vt <- function(V){
  rnorm(1,0,sqrt(V))
}

func_Theta_t <- function(t,Theta_t1,wt) { # Theta_t1 is Theta_{t-1}
  func_Gt(t)*Theta_t1 + wt
}


Then we simulated \(F_t\) and the below plots show the generated data and I used a density plot to see if the data was what I expected, and it is distributed correctly. I then also generated the the starting \(\theta_0\) value.

Ft <- round(Ft,1)
plot(Ft, type = "o")

Code

Theta_0 |> signif(3)


[1] 0.0798


Then I made a function for generated the observations (the \(y_t\)) and tested it worked as expected which it did.


Code
func_yt <- function(Ft,t,vt,Theta_t){

}

yt <- c()
vt <- func_vt(V)

Then I made lists and a loop to simulate the 100 states and observations.


Code

Theta <- c()
Theta_t1 <- Theta_0

for (t in 1:100) { 
  vt <- func_vt(V)

Figure 12.1 below shows the underlying state as well as the observations.


Code
par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))
plot(Y, type = "l", lwd = 1.5, col = "darkgrey",
     main = "Simulated State and Observations",

lines(Theta, lwd = 2, col = "darkred")
legend("topright", legend = c("Y_t", "Theta_t"),
       col = c("darkgrey", "darkred"), lwd = c(1.5, 2))








Figure 12.1: Simulated observations \(Y_t\) (grey) and true state \(\theta_t\) (dark red), with \(V = 2\), \(W = 1\).





The observations in Figure 12.1 closely follow the state line, but have more variance.


12.2.2 Q2 - Kalman Filter
Then I built the Kalman Filter and checked it worked as intended using the first observation.


Code
m0 <- 0
C0 <- 1

Gt <- as.matrix(func_Gt(t=1))
Wt <- as.matrix(W)

# Gt
# Wt

Rt <- Gt %*% C0 %*% t(Gt)+ Wt
at <- Gt %*% m0

# Rt
# at

Vt <- as.matrix(V)
ft <- Ft[1] %*% at
Qt <- Ft[1] %*% Rt %*% t(Ft[1]) + Vt

# Vt |> round(3)
# ft |> round(3)
# Qt |> round(3)

Kt <-  Rt %*% t(Ft[1]) %*% solve(Qt)
yt <- Y[1]
et <- yt - ft
mt <- at + Kt %*% et
Ct <- Rt - Kt %*% Ft[1] %*% Rt

# Kt |> round(3)
# yt |> round(3)
# et |> round(3)
# mt |> round(3)
# Ct |> round(3)

round(c(R = Rt, a = at, f = ft, Q = Qt, K = Kt, e = et, m = mt, C = Ct), 3)


    R     a     f     Q     K     e     m     C 
1.250 0.000 0.000 2.800 0.357 1.891 0.675 0.893 


Happy with the values above, we then convert the Kalman Filter code for one observation into a loop that can be applied to the entire dataset. Figure 12.2 below shows the true state and the estimated state using the Kalman Filter and our inital values of \(V = 2\) and \(W = 1\).


Code
m0 <- 0
C0 <- 1
m_t1 <- m0
C_t1 <- C0

m <- c()
C <- c()
a <- c()
R <- c()
f <- c()
Q <- c()
e <- c()

for (t in 1:100) {
  Gt <- as.matrix(func_Gt(t))
  Wt <- as.matrix(W)
  Rt <- Gt %*% C_t1 %*% t(Gt) + Wt
  at <- Gt %*% m_t1

  Vt <- as.matrix(V)
  ft <- Ft[t] %*% at
  Qt <- Ft[t] %*% Rt %*% t(Ft[t]) + Vt

  Kt <- Rt %*% t(Ft[t]) %*% solve(Qt)
  yt <- Y[t]
  et <- yt - ft
  mt <- at + Kt %*% et
  Ct <- Rt - Kt %*% Ft[t] %*% Rt

  m <- c(m, mt)
  C <- c(C, Ct)
  a <- c(a, at)
  R <- c(R, Rt)
  f <- c(f, ft)
  Q <- c(Q, Qt)
  e <- c(e, et)

  m_t1 <- mt
  C_t1 <- Ct
}

plot(Theta, type = "l", col = "darkred")
lines(m, col = "blue")








Figure 12.2: Simulated observations \(Y_t\) (grey), true state \(\theta_t\) (dark red) and Kalman filter estimate \(m_t\) (blue), with \(V = 2\), \(W = 1\).





The red line in Figure 12.2 above has more variation, but the blue estimate line follows the same general patterns.
Now we know the filter is working, we use Figure 12.3 below to compare the observations, the underlying true state and the Kalman Fitler estimate of the states.


Code
par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))
plot(Y, type = "l", lwd = 1.5, col = "darkgrey",
     main = "Kalman Filter Estimate of the State",
     ylab = "Value", xlab = "Period t",
     ylim = c(-5, 6), las = 1, bty = "l",
     cex.main = 1.1, font.main = 1)
abline(h = 0, col = "grey", lty = 2)
lines(Theta, lwd = 2, col = "darkred")
lines(m, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue")
legend("topright", legend = c("Y_t", "Theta_t", "m_t"),
       col = c("darkgrey", "darkred", "steelblue"), lwd = c(1.5, 2, 2))








Figure 12.3: Simulated observations \(Y_t\) (grey), true state \(\theta_t\) (dark red) and Kalman filter estimate \(m_t\) (blue), with \(V = 2\), \(W = 1\).





Both state lines in Figure 12.3 follow the ocilating pattern of the observations. The red true state is slightly smoother than the observations, and the Kalman Filter estimate is the smoothest of the three.
Then we turn our Kalman Filter loop code into a function in order to use optim() to fine the Maximum Likelihood Estimates (MLE) for V and W.


Code
func_Kalman_Filter <- function(Y,Ft,m0,C0,params){
  V <- params[1]
  W <- params[2]
  
  m_t1 <- m0
  C_t1 <- C0
  
  m <- c()
  C <- c()
  a <- c()
  R <- c()
  f <- c()
  Q <- c()
  e <- c()
  
  for (t in 1:length(Y)) {
    Gt <- as.matrix(func_Gt(t))
    Wt <- as.matrix(W)
    Rt <- Gt %*% C_t1 %*% t(Gt) + Wt
    at <- Gt %*% m_t1
  
    Vt <- as.matrix(V)
    ft <- Ft[t] %*% at
    Qt <- Ft[t] %*% Rt %*% t(Ft[t]) + Vt
  
    yt <- Y[t]
    if (is.na(yt)) {          # accounting for missing values for question 3
      et <- NA
      mt <- at
      Ct <- Rt
    } else {
      Kt <- Rt %*% t(Ft[t]) %*% solve(Qt)
      et <- yt - ft
      mt <- at + Kt %*% et
      Ct <- Rt - Kt %*% Ft[t] %*% Rt
    }
  
    m <- c(m, mt)
    C <- c(C, Ct)
    a <- c(a, at)
    R <- c(R, Rt)
    f <- c(f, ft)
    Q <- c(Q, Qt)
    e <- c(e, et)
  
    m_t1 <- mt
    C_t1 <- Ct
  }
  
  neg_loglik <- 0.5 * sum(log(Q) + e^2 / Q, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  return(list(m = m, C = C, a = a, R = R, f = f, Q = Q, e = e, neg_loglik = neg_loglik))
}


We then run new function and create Figure 12.4, which is the same plot as Figure 12.3 above to make sure the results from our function are the same.


Code
m0 <- 0
C0 <- 1

V <- 2
W <- 1
params <- c(V,W)

KF <- func_Kalman_Filter(Y,Ft,m0,C0,params) #(Y,Ft,m0,C0,params)




Code
par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))
plot(Theta, type = "l", pch = 16, cex = 0.6, lwd = 1.5, col = "darkred",
     main = "Simulated State and Kalman Filter Estimate",
     ylab = "State", xlab = "Period t",
     ylim = c(-4, 5), las = 1, bty = "l",
     cex.main = 1.1, font.main = 1)
abline(h = 0, col = "grey", lty = 2)
lines(KF$m, type = "l", pch = 1, cex = 0.6, lwd = 1.5, col = "steelblue")
legend("topright", legend = c("Simulated state Theta_t", "KF estimate m_t"),
       col = c("darkred", "steelblue"), lwd = 1.5)








Figure 12.4: Simulated values of the state \(\theta_t\) (dark red) and their Kalman filter estimates \(\hat\theta_t = m_t\) (blue), with known \(V = 2\), \(W = 1\) (cf. Meinhold and Singpurwalla, 1983, Figure 2).





The lines in Figure 12.4 above show that the function is working as intended, and we are ready to find the MLEs.
We then make a function that only outputs the negative log-likelihood from our Kalman Filter function, and make sure that the parameters being optimised are combined into the first argument in the function.


Code
func_neg_loglik <- function(params, Y, Ft, m0, C0) { # puts params in front for optim, and puts V and W in log scale
  func_Kalman_Filter(Y, Ft, m0, C0, exp(params))$neg_loglik
}


Then we apply optim to our negative log-likelihood function, and check results.


Code
V <- 2
W <- 1
params <- log(c(V,W))
optim_est <- optim(params, func_neg_loglik,
                   Y = Y, Ft = Ft, m0 = m0, C0 = C0, hessian = TRUE)

optim_est$convergence |> round(3)


[1] 0


Code
exp(optim_est$par) |> round(4)


[1] 1.5761 1.3909


Code
optim_est$value |> round(3)


[1] 105.915


We confirm the optim function converged as the convergence is \(= 0\). The estimates are \(V = 1.5761\) and \(W = 1.3909\). The overall negative log-likelihood score is \(= 105.915\). We compare this score below with the obtained when using our initial values for V and W.


Code
KF$neg_loglik |> round(3)


[1] 106.158


When \(V = 2\) and \(W = 1\), our negative log-likelihood score was slightly 106.158. This is slightly worse than the score achieved by our best estimates, despite them being the true values. In this one realisation of the data, the true estimates do not fit the data as well as the MLEs.


12.2.3 Q3 - Forecasting
When then use our Kalman Filter Function to make forecasts for the next 5 periods by adding new random values for \(F_t\), and \(NA\) values for \(Y\). We also create the prediction intervals for state predictions.

Ft_h <- round(rnorm(h, 1, 0.2), 1)
Ft_forecast <- c(Ft, Ft_h)
Y_forecast  <- c(Y, rep(NA, h))

Forecasts <- data.frame(t = Forecast_slots, forecast = KF_forecast$f[Forecast_slots], lower = KF_forecast$f[Forecast_slots] - 1.96 * sqrt(KF_forecast$Q[Forecast_slots]), upper = KF_forecast$f[Forecast_slots] + 1.96 * sqrt(KF_forecast$Q[Forecast_slots]))

The forecasts shown in the table above will be used in our plots in question 4 below.


12.2.4 Q4 - Plotting
We now combine everything we have so far in Figure 12.5 below.


Code
par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))
plot(Y, type = "l", lwd = 1.5, col = "darkgrey",
     main = "Data with Fitted, Filtered and Forecast Values",
     ylab = "Value", xlab = "Period t",
     xlim = c(1, 105), ylim = c(-5, 7), las = 1, bty = "l",
     cex.main = 1.1, font.main = 1)
abline(h = 0, col = "grey", lty = 2)
abline(v = 100.5, col = "grey40", lty = 3)
lines(KF_forecast$f, lwd = 2, col = "darkorange")

       legend = c("Observations Y_t", "Fitted / forecast f_t",
                  "Filtered m_t", "95% prediction interval"),
       col = c("darkgrey", "darkorange", "steelblue", "darkorange"),
       lwd = c(1.5, 2, 2, 1.5), lty = c(1, 1, 1, 2), cex = 0.85)








Figure 12.5: Observations \(Y_t\) (grey), one-step-ahead fitted values and forecasts \(f_t\) (orange), filtered state estimates \(m_t\) (blue), and 95% prediction intervals for \(h = 1, \dots, 5\) (dashed), using the ML estimates \(\hat V = 1.58\), \(\hat W = 1.39\). The vertical line marks the end of the observed data.





The orange fitted line in Figure 12.5 above is our forecasts before seeing the observation, and then the filtered blue line lies between the fitted line and the grey observation line. The additonal information updates our estimate of the underlying state. The 5 forecast state values are show in orange. As the function updates the forecasts but the Kalamn Gain function \(= 0\) as there are no new observations, and the line trends toward 0. The 95% prediction intervals are shown alongside the forecasts. They interval is very wide due to the high variation and oscillation in the data, making our estimates very uncertain.


12.2.5 Q5 - ACF
We then standardise our residuals and check that them for any patterns or dependence in Figure 12.6 below.


Code
residuals <- KF_forecast$e[1:100]
standardised_res <- residuals / sqrt(KF_forecast$Q[1:100])

par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))
plot(standardised_res, type = "h", lwd = 1.5, col = "steelblue",
     main = "Standardised Residuals",
     ylab = "Residual", xlab = "Period t",
     ylim = c(-3, 3), las = 1, bty = "l",
     cex.main = 1.1, font.main = 1)
abline(h = 0, col = "grey")
abline(h = c(-1.96, 1.96), col = "grey", lty = 2)








Figure 12.6: Standardised one-step-ahead prediction errors \(e_t/\sqrt{Q_t}\) over time. The dashed lines mark \(\pm 1.96\).





The residuals in Figure 12.6 above appear random. Next we will check for correlation using an ACF plot in Figure 12.7 below.


Code
par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))
acf(standardised_res, main = "ACF of Standardised Residuals",
    las = 1, bty = "l", cex.main = 1.1, font.main = 1)








Figure 12.7: Sample ACF of the standardised residuals. The dashed blue lines are approximate 95% bounds for white noise.





Figure 12.7 clearly shows that there is no significant correlation in the first 20 lags, as all the spikes lie within the blue dotted line. We can confirm this by checking the mean and vairance of the standardised residuals, as well as a Ljung-Box test.


Code
mean(standardised_res) |> round(3)


[1] -0.027


Code
var(standardised_res) |> round(3)


[1] 1.01


Code
Box.test(standardised_res, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")



    Box-Ljung test

data:  standardised_res
X-squared = 6.4481, df = 10, p-value = 0.7763


The residuals have a mean of 0 and and a variance of 1, and the Ljung-Box test shows that there is not enough evidence to suggest there is dependence between the residuals. Our Kalman Filter has managed to capture the time dependent underlying state to the extend that the remaining unexplained variance is essential white noise.


12.2.6 Q6 - Results
We have successfully built our Kalman Filter and applied it to our simulated data. The maximum likelihood estimates fit this one simulated series slightly better than the true values, but they split the noise differently between the two equations.

title: 12  Project 4: Kalman filter simulation study
text:
12.3 Reflection
This was the most technical project in the portfolio, and the one I was most proud of when it worked. Most of the difficulty was in small mistakes that I could only find by plotting. My first simulation drew the state twice in each step, so the observations and the state did not match. I fixed this by generating the noise once and passing it into the functions. I also gave rnorm() the variance instead of the standard deviation, and in the filter I first used a random draw \(w_t\) where the formula needs the variance \(W\), which gave a negative \(R_t\). Using all of Ft instead of Ft[t], and t(Q) instead of solve(Q), caused similar errors.
The slides use matrix notation, and it took me a while to see that my state has size one, so the same formulas apply and only the dimensions change. The slides also do not show how to estimate \(V\) and \(W\). I had to work out that the filter’s one-step prediction errors give the likelihood, and why optim() works better on the log scale, where the variances cannot become negative. Matching the paper’s notation to the slides was another hurdle: the paper’s \(\hat\theta_t\) and \(\Sigma_t\) are the slides’ \(m_t\) and \(C_t\).
At first the wide prediction intervals felt pointless, but they reflect how noisy the data is and how quickly the state forgets its past. The biggest lesson was that the estimates can fit the data well without recovering the true parameters, because \(V\) and \(W\) are hard to separate in a single short series.

title: 13  Journal
text:
Introduction
The journal entries below were not written on the exact dates listed. They are created with hindsight and by using all notes taken throughout the course. I take many notes as I work through course material, including personal thoughts and reflections. This allowed me to create after the fact, what I personally think is a better representation of my thoughts and experiences of the course, than would be achieved by writing journal entries as they happen. For example, despite only learning of the need for keeping a journal when the portfolio was introduced in week 4, I was able to accurately present the weeks prior to that. This journal captures my general weekly thoughts, mostly around what we did in lectures. More specific thoughts related to work done for the Portfolio, including the the four mini projects and the work done on each course content section, are contained within each of those sections.
I am very proud of my journal below. It is very personal and unique to me and who I am, and I hope trust it provides a true insight into one person’s experience of this course.

title: 13  Journal
text:
Section 1

27 July 2026 - Week 1 - Introduction
This week we were introduced to the Time Series (TS) course. While I’m still uncertain if I will continue to stick with the course or not, I enjoyed the introduction, and I can see myself probably not dropping it. The course looks very organised and well structured. Although this is not certain, as I still have around 6 other courses I intend to attend the lectures of this week.
Assuming I will stick with the course, my initial thoughts are as follows. Time is a very important factor in many types of data analysis, and so far I’ve only imagined plugging in time \(t\) as a variable in a regression analysis. This first lecture introduced us to a new kind (or class) of data, called a Time Series Object. I am very excited as this new data class unlocks the ability to use many packages and functions in R which I have not heard of before. I feel like I will be well equipped to apply my statistical skills in more fields and situations with having knowledge of TS objects.
Before the next lecture, I need to see the TSA_intro file on Amathuba, install prerequisite packages and look at the “ts()” function. See Chapter 1.


3 August 2026 - Week 2 - Autoregressive Models (ARIMA)
This week we started exploring simple models that are used in Time Series, those being autoregressive models.
We learned the foundations first, like the notation and different types of time series data, and the importance of why order matters in time series data to see dependence through time. This is what separates TS data from what we’ve seen before, where the data is usually assumed to be independent, and identically distributed. In TS, the data is not independent. We then learnt about forecasting, and how the further into the future the forecast the more uncertain it is.
We learned how to explore time series data using classical decomposition. That is when you break down your data into four components, the trend, seasonality, cycle, and the irregular component which is what is leftover after estimating the other 3 components.
Finally we were introduced to benchmarks and forecast accuracy. The benchmark models that our models have to beat are the mean, naive, seasonal naive, and drift models.
While the concepts have felt simple so far, I am struggling to understand the context. We were shown the classical decomposition formula, and then a bunch of example plots for both additive and multiplicative form. The problem is, I feel like I don’t understand the bigger picture yet. What are we even modelling? How do these different components work? I have a small base understanding of SARIMA and its parts from past experience, but the different terms that make it up haven’t been referenced yet, and I don’t see how it relates to the decomposed components. Hopefully this will become clearer over the coming lectures, but right now I’m not sure where we are heading.
Next up I must read ahead in the slides up until slide 83.
See Chapter 2 for practical application done on ARIMA models.


17 August 2026 - Week 4 - Portfolio and ARIMA continued
There was no lecture last week. Will be made up at some stage.
Today started off with being introduced to the Portfolio, which will be used in place of tests or assignments, and will be integral in our oral exam later.
I will keep this short, but wow this is overwhelming. The flexibility in choosing substantial projects sounds nice but I don’t have a clue how to approach these yet. I personally like structure, and while there are no set deadlines for submission, this presents a personal challenge to me. For example, while always hating them, I thrive with weekly tutorials as opposed to something like this, which is much bigger and more open ended.
The positive is that if handled correctly, this should be a more fun, pressure free experience. There will also be multiple opportunities for feedback, so that should provide more direction.
We need to submit our first substantial project idea on 5 September before the vac, so that it can be approved. Then the first draft of the first project will be submitted on 13 Sep for feedback. I need to be diligent and work consistently on this, otherwise I foresee it being difficult to balance this along with my Honours Project.
After being introduced to the portfolio, we continued with ARIMA models. First we briefly looked at how to use TS objects in R, although this will be something we have to go through more in depth alone. See Chapter 2.
We looked at cross validation for Time Series, and how we can’t split the data at random due to their dependence. Rather, you have to split the data into training and validation sets, where the validation is at least as long as the amount of time you intend to use the model to forecast for. You then apply accuracy measures (such as RMSE) to compare the model predictions vs the validation set.
We also learned of three validation strategies, but this was very confusing. The three methods are Walk-Forward, Expanding, and Sliding, but seems to be no difference between walk forward and expanding. The example plots in the slides are identical. Slides will be updated to clarify, but how they are described as being different while the plots and math equations looking identical is very confusing.
We then learned about the lag operator and stationary, which introduced the ARIMA form. I now see that this doesn’t relate perfectly to classical decomposition, which is more about seeing whats in the data, more than modelling it like ARIMA. While this made sense in theory, how we apply ARIMA in R will be explained in a lab after we have finished the section 1 lectures. The goal is to find a model that gives an error term that looks like white noise.
Then we looked at liner models for the conditional mean. Here we learned about the different parts of ARIMA, being the MA(q) model, the AR(p) model, and ARMA(p,q) models. the I in ARIMA stands for differencing. Once a model is applied, the autocovariance and autocorrelation structure is analysed using ACF and PACF plots, which can be used to identify what model may be most suitable, from white noise, to ARMA(p,q).
See Chapter 2 for Exercise 1.


24 August 2026 - Week 5 - ARIMA continued
First we were shown where to find some data sets to use in our substantial projects.
Then we learned to use the difference operator (I) to remove trends from non-stationary data to turn them into stationary data for our ARMA models. We now have the full picture for ARIMA(q,d,q). ARIMA forecasts use the past level, past change, and past error. We then used residuals to help determine if there is a better model to fit the data. Seasonal components were added to make SARIMA models with the form SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q).
See Chapter 2 for coding SARIMA.
Next we must read up on ARCH/GARCH models for next week.


31 August 2026 - Week 6 - ARIMA continued
Today we learned how to get things done in R for ARIMA models.
This was useful as a reminder of what we had covered so far, and in seeing how it fits together when it comes to applying it and writing the code.
I personally really struggled with this lecture, as it was not a lab session, despite it going through a lot of coding. This is fine on its own, but it went very fast, and introduced many functions without going into much detail how they worked.
It went into detail on the different packages available for TS objects, and gave examples on different kinds of datasets that can be analysed. It also gave a good run through of how one may do a full time series analysis, which will be very useful to use as a guide when doing the first substantial project (see Chapter 9). It covered both the data preparation through an EDA, and the modelling process. It would have been great to have gone through these slides much slower, with the code adding context to the theory, so I must be sure to do so myself in my own time. I wish I could’ve kept up by following along during the lecture on a computer though.
This was the last lecture before the one week vac, and we hadn’t spoken more about the first substantial project. 16 September 2026 - Week 7 - ARCH/GARCH
First week after the vac, we had a make up lecture in the lab to make up for the missed lecture in week 3 to discuss ARCH & GARCH models (volatility models). These are commonly used in financial returns data which have conditional heteroskedasticity, which means that the variance in the data isn’t constant across the observed time period. There are periods of higher or lower volatility, or in other words, the variance depends on time \(t\). This is the variance equation, which describes the conditional variance at \(t\). This is used along with the mean equation, which describes the predictable component of a time series, to model the data. The mean equation can either be constant, or it ca be an ARMA model.
We learned to transform the data into the appropriate variable of interest, which is usually logarithmic return. We learned about the error terms (or innovations), which are used in our models.
Then we learned about the models themselves, starting with ARCH. The ARCH(q) model models the variance by summing up the squared past \(q\) error terms. GARCH(p,q) models then add a lagged conditional variance term, which makes the variance dependent on the past \(p\) variances. GARCH is used when volatility persists for an extended period. Persistence refers to how many periods it takes for the effect of a shock to disappear.
We also learned to identify if an ARCH or GARCH model may be needed by using an ARCH LM test to see if residuals (error terms) are dependent. We looked at several diagnostics to determine if an adequate model has been selected. Finally, we were introduced to the rugarch package, and were given some practical exercise questions (see Chapter 3).

title: 13  Journal
text:
Section 2

14 September 2026 - Week 7 - Exponential Smoothing
Rewinding a week, we started section two of the course after the vac, beginning with Exponential Smoothing, also known as exponetially weighted moving average.
This section was very confusing, as, like spectral analysis, it stepped away from ARIMA, and I struggled to figure out how the actual model itself works. The model works using a smoothing equation to find the level \(l_t\), and then that is used in the forecast equation \(\hat{y}_{t+h|t} = l_t\). But \(l_t\) is a recursive function as it refers to \(l_{t-1}\), so it’s hard to picture had it’s calculated when you have to use the entire data set. The resulting plot examples also also seem to be equivalent to the naive model, where every prediction is equal to the actual value right before it.
I did mange to grasp it, and will also have to code it (see Chapter 5) which will be a challenge but I think I’ll manage. We learned about different smoothing parameters (values of \(\alpha\)), and how that effects both how the model fits the data, and how it effects forecasts and confidence intervals.
Regarding the portfolios, we also got told to reduce the scope of each mini project, and that we can use the exercises from each section as the mini project, which is a big relief!
Then we used Holt’s method to add a linear trend equation to our forecast and level equations, as well as when to use additive or multiplicative models. We also learned about ETS to determine exactly which method best fits our data.
Then we learned the difference between prediction intervals and confidence intervals, and the prediction uncertainty is greater than the confidence interval as it relates to a model parameter not just an estimate, which also accounts for uncertainty in your model choice. We also learned about forecasting error to use in our prediction intervals.
Then we were introduced to state space models for exponential smoothing, where we are interested in the underlying state behind our observations, which are produced by our state plus some random noise. Lastly we looked at using bootstrapping to create prediction intervals, and bayesian predictions.
It definitely took me some time to get my head around the levels and recursion, but with some practice I think I’ll get it just fine.


21 September 2026 - Week 8 - Time Series Regression
In this lecture we learned about using time series regression models, which are useful when we want to understand how are data came to be as it is, rather than forecasting which ARIMA focuses on.
In TS Regression, we have a normal linear regression model, but instead of the error terms being i.i.d and normally distributed, they are replaced by ARMA errors to account for the auto-correlation between errors. The error term \(v_t\) is dependent on the past error term in the form \(v_t = \phi v_{t-1} + e_t\). This means there are now 2 “error” terms, and the objective is to minimise SSE of the \(e_t\) errors.
We also learned about using generalized least squares to add an AR1 process for errors in R, and about interventions to improved the regression model.
We then looked at harmonic regression which is used for seasonal effects, but this was very difficult to follow at the time as it required an understanding of spectral analysis (which we only got introduced to in an informal lab session later that same week). You can use a sum of sin and cosine functions to model and cyclic time series, and look at the spectrum to see which frequencies explain most of the variation in the data.
We also saw that time series regression could be used in generalized additive models (GAMs), not just simple linear models by using splines, which allow for different error correlation structures. GAMs are useful when dealing with non-linear trends.
We will have to show how to calculate the \(e_t\) terms by hand (see Chapter 6), and will be given data to fit our models too.
I really enjoyed this section, as it brought together my understanding of time series data and combined it with what I’m already familiar with. I’m excited to try make a linear regression model, and to compare it with and without using ARMA errors.


28 September 2026 - Week 9 - State Space Models
This week we looked at State Space Models (SSMs). In state space models, we aren’t interested in the observations, but rather we are interested in some underlying unobservable signal that generates the observation. In other words, the observations are a function of a hidden state plus some noise, and we want to estimate the hidden state at different points in time.
This was a bit confusing at first to conceptualise, but once we were shown a directed acyclic graph, and an example plot which showed the “hidden” state that observations were produced from, it became much more clear. The variable of interest is the state, not the observations. The observations are independent of each other, and ony depend on the state at that time. The states are only dependent on the state immediately before it.
The state space model uses an observation equation, which is a function of the state, and a state equation, which is a function of the previous state. We focused on three special SSMs, which are the Random Walk plus Noise, Local Linear Trend, and the Basic Structural Model. We were shown examples and some practical code. Finally, we ended off with regression with time varying coefficients, by adding explanatory variables to the observation equation. We will look at Kalman Filters next week.
There is a prac to do and a tutorial. See Chapter 7. This section definitely looks the most challenging technically so far, so I need to make sure I practice. I haven’t kept up with the exercises and practice so far, and I’m running short on time, and the Honours Project is due soon.


5 October 2026 - Week 10 - Kalman Filter
The Kalman Filter is used to help find estimates for the underlying signal in a state space model. It works like a baesian approach, where we predict the state (the prior), predict the observation (the likelihood), and then update the state estimate after seeing the next observation (the posterior).
The algorithm used is a bit complicated, and it’s a bit unclear exactly how it relates to Bayes. In Bayes you take a prior distribution, and then multiply by the likelihood given the data. In the Kalman Filter, you update one observation at a time. You find the difference between your estimate of the observation and the actual observation (the error), and use that to adjust your belief of the underlying distribution. The adjustment is the error multiplied by the Kalman Gain. The Kalman Gain is calculated using the one step ahead predictive distributions. If the gain is equal to 0, the posterior will equal the prior no matter what the error is. This occurs when there are missing (or NA) values in the data.
This is all very confusing, and will hopefully make more sense once I work through it. See Chapter 7.
We can use likelihood to estimate the two variance parameters, the variance of the two error terms. One is from the variance of the observation equation errors, and the other is from the state equation error variance.
We also have the Kalman Smoother, which works in reverse. It starts by using the Kalman Filter estimate of the state after looking at all the observations, and then recursively steps back through each estimate and smooths them out. The filter estimates follow the observations too much, and by smoothing it out, you get a smoother, better estimate of the underlying state.
I still have to do the following in Chapter 7. I need to write the equations in full and program the Kalman Filter, and get CIs and PIs. There is also the tutorial and practical questions. This section definitely involved more maths than the other sections, and some of the recursive formulas are hard to follow, but I think coding it will help me understand how they work. I’m also seriously stressed now about the Portfolio and the mini projects.


12 October 2026 - Week 11 - Hidden Markov Models
Is this the last lecture? I can’t believe how fast the year has flown by. The last section in the course outline is Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and we finished the slides on it in this lecture.
Like State Space Models, Hidden Markov models are interested in the underlying state or data generating process, but can only observe the data. The difference is that in Markov models, the underlying states are discrete and finite. This is nicely illustrated using a transition diagram of a coin toss example.
In addition to a transition diagram, we can make a transition probability matrix (TPM) to the the probabilities of the state staying or moving to each other state. The hidden states have to be discrete, but the observations (or outcomes) can be discrete or continuous.
This works very similarly to SSMs, so I found the concept fairly easy to grasp initially. The math was a bit harder to understand how it worked in this context. The joint probability is equal to the product of the conditional probabilities. In the Directed Acyclic Graph, this means the joint probability of the nodes is the product of the conditional probability of all nodes conditional on their parent nodes.
We looked at mixture models which were the sum of multiple underlying distributions. These relate to HMMs when we have a dependent mixture model, the probability of being in a state at time \(t\) depends on the state at time \(t-1\). You multiply state probability by the conditional probabilities of an observation, sum them all up and take the product over all observations to get the likelihood.
In HMM we have a transition probability, and an emission (or observation) probability. With some very complex math, we use likelihood to estimate the transition probability matrix and the parameters of each states distribution. We looked using likelihood at first a single observation, then with two observations.
The math in this section is a bit beyond me, but I understand how the HMM works and when it gets used. The tutorial exercises will help me practice applying the math by hand, but I’m confident I can do the appropriate coding in R. See Chapter 8.
We can also use one of the exercises in this weeks tut as one of our mini projects, but I’m not sure which one as the tut doesn’t specify. We can just simulate data, fit the model, and then decode it. I think I won’t need it anyway so it’s probably fine.

title: 14  Reflective commentary
text:
14.1 Learning achievements
In this section, I summarise and reflect on the Time Series course, the contents, and the portfolio.
When the course started, I had only ever imagined time as a variable plugged into a regression. The first thing I had to learn was that time series data is different: the order matters and the observations are not independent. Much of what followed made sense in theory but only clicked once I coded it. ARIMA felt confusing on the slides, with its recursive formulas and lag notation, but fitting models and reading the ACF and PACF made it concrete.
Each section changed how I looked at the data. GARCH was not the small extension of ARIMA I expected. It moved the focus from the mean to the volatility, and in Project 2 (Chapter 10) the mean equation became a constant. Spectral analysis only made sense when I thought of a piano chord: three notes combine into one signal, and the periodogram splits it back into its frequencies. Exponential smoothing felt like the first time a model found the underlying level rather than copying the last value. State space models and the Kalman filter were the most technical part of the course. Coding the filter myself for Project 4 (Chapter 12), and seeing it work, was the moment I was most proud of. Hidden Markov models then felt like a natural step, with discrete states instead of a continuous one.
Project 3 (Chapter 11) brought these ideas together with regression, which I already knew. The most important thing I learned there was that the error model has to come before the choice of regressors, because autocorrelated errors make every extra term look more useful than it is.

title: 14  Reflective commentary
text:
14.2 How the sections connect
Looking back, the sections are more connected than they felt while I was learning them. Exponential smoothing introduced the idea of an underlying level that the observations scatter around, and state space models made that idea formal, with a hidden state and a Kalman filter that updates it as each observation arrives. Hidden Markov models use the same structure, but with a finite set of discrete states instead of a continuous one. Seeing this chain made the later sections much easier than they would have been on their own.
Spectral analysis and time series regression also turned out to be linked. The harmonic terms in regression are the same sine and cosine waves that the periodogram picks out, but used as regressors in the time domain. I first confused the two, and separating them helped me understand both. GARCH, in turn, showed me that modelling the mean is not the only goal: for returns the mean is almost unpredictable, and the useful information is in how the variance changes.
The projects helped me see these links in practice. Projects 1 and 3 use the same Eskom data, first with a SARIMA model and then with a regression with ARMA errors. Comparing them showed me how much a held-out test set, a lockdown dummy and a careful choice of error model matter, and that a model which explains the data well does not always forecast better. Project 4 made the Kalman filter concrete in a way the formulas alone never did.

title: 14  Reflective commentary
text:
14.3 Methodological challenges
The biggest challenges were conceptual rather than coding. I struggled with the three validation strategies, because walk-forward and expanding windows looked identical in the slides. Recursion was hard to picture in moving average and autoregressive models, and again in exponential smoothing, where each level depends on the one before it. Spectral analysis was difficult because we worked straight from complex lab code before seeing any theory, so I had to go back and find simpler examples myself.
In Project 4 I made several mistakes I could only find by plotting. My first simulation drew the state twice in each step, so the observations and the state did not match. I gave rnorm() a variance when it needs a standard deviation, and I used a random draw where the filter needed the variance W. The matrix notation in the slides took me a long time to connect to my one-dimensional case. In Project 2 I first thought skewed t errors and GJR-GARCH did the same job, until I saw that one describes the shape of the errors and the other how the variance reacts to the sign of a shock. I also found that rugarch labels its EGARCH parameters differently from my notes, so I learned to check formulas rather than trust names. When the residual tests still showed some dependence, I reported it as a limitation instead of hiding it.
Real data brought its own problems. The Eskom data had about a year of missing demand values, a sharp dip during the 2020 lockdown, and the question of whether to model the daily or the weekly maximum. The exchange rate data had three days where the price glitched, which created six extreme returns. Plotting the raw data before modelling caught both problems.

title: 14  Reflective commentary
text:
14.4 Ethics and reproducibility
I tried to make the work reproducible. Each project uses a fixed seed where there is simulation, the exchange rate data is saved to a file so the results don’t change when Yahoo updates, and the whole portfolio is one Quarto project with the data and code included (Appendix B). I also tried to be honest about the limits of my data. Under load-shedding, Eskom’s observed demand is partly suppressed supply rather than true demand, and planned outages are scheduled around expected demand, so their coefficient is an association, not a cause. I removed six extreme returns in Project 2 because they came from price glitches, but a more careful analysis would check them against real market events. My use of AI is described in Appendix A.

title: 14  Reflective commentary
text:
14.5 Future development
The hardest part of this course was not the content but the structure. I thrive with weekly tutorials and deadlines, and this portfolio, like my Honours Project, was open-ended. I procrastinated, fell behind, and did much of the work in the last two weeks. The main thing I would change is to set my own deadlines from the start and work on the portfolio every week. On the technical side, I want to strengthen my mathematical foundations, especially likelihoods and the matrix form of the Kalman filter. I also want to finish what I had to drop, writing my own GARCH likelihood, testing for a structural break around 2020, and evaluating all my forecasts out of sample, starting with a proper test set for Project 1.

title: 14  Reflective commentary
text:
14.6 Conclusions
This course changed how I think about data. I started by treating time as just another variable, and I finish it understanding that the dependence between observations is the main thing to model, whether through the mean, the variance, a hidden state or the errors of a regression. The eight sections felt separate at first, but they share a small set of ideas: an underlying process we cannot see directly, observations that are a noisy realisation of it, and models that try to separate the two.
The four projects were where this understanding became my own. Working with real Eskom and exchange rate data taught me that most of the effort goes into checking, cleaning and justifying choices before any model is fitted, and that an honest limitation is worth more than a result that looks perfect. Coding the Kalman filter and the regression estimates myself showed me what the packages are doing.
I did not manage my time as well as I should have, and some parts of the portfolio, especially Project 1, are less complete than I would like. But I understand far more than I did at the start of the course, and I know which areas I want to strengthen next.
Overall, I really enjoyed this course. It gave me a great opportunity to learn not just about a new type of data and how to model it, but also about myself, my strengths and weaknesses, and I got to practice some good life skills. In the end, I finished my portfolio on time, and I am very proud of it.

title: Appendix A — AI disclosure
text:
Declaration of use of generative AI
I used Claude (Anthropic), during the preparation of this portfolio. It was used in a supporting role, to help me understand course material and statistical concepts, to help with R coding and troubleshooting, and to help with the structure and formatting of the Quarto book. On some occasions Claude wrote or ran code, which I reviewed, tested and adapted before using it. I used Claude-written example files for each topic as reference material to see what each section needed, and wrote the portfolio content myself. Claude also helped assemble the reflective commentary (Chapter 14) from my own journal entries and section reflections, which I then edited.
The choice of projects, data, models and methods, the analysis and its interpretation, and all written reflections and commentary are my own. Where AI-assisted code or explanations informed the work, I checked them against the course notes and my own output.

All the data files used in this portfolio are included in the data/ folder, so nothing needs to be downloaded to reproduce the results.
